- [Multimodal pre-processing](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/chat-completions/multimodal-pre-processing.md) runs afterwards, so media descriptions are not moderated.

## Scope

In `LayeredGuardrail` mode, the safeguard evaluates the conversation history, not only the latest message. Moderation applies only to input text:

- Generated output is not moderated.
- Images, audio, video, and file contents are not analyzed. The safeguard receives only a marker indicating that media was present.
- Tool or worker authorization still requires application-level policy; moderation is not an authorization mechanism.

Use moderation for broad safety policy. Use workers when the decision depends on external identity, account state, or business-specific policy.

For when self-assessment is enough and when the separate safeguard stays necessary, with timings from live runs, see [LLM moderation API: separate layer or model self-assessment?](https://aivax.net/blog/aivax-gateway-moderation/).

---

Source: https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/chat-completions/function-interpreter.html

# Function interpreter (deprecated)

> **Deprecated.** The function interpreter is kept only for existing gateways. Do not use it in new gateways. Choose a model with native tool calling instead; the **Models** page of the dashboard lists which models support it.

The function interpreter, also called the tool handler, adds tool calling to models that do not produce reliable native tool calls. Instead of sending the tool definitions to the provider, AIVAX asks the model to choose a tool in a text format and converts its answer into a tool call. Configure it in **Tool calling handler** in the gateway editor or in `parameters.knownToolHandlerName`.

## Values

| Value | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `native` or `null` | Uses the model's native tool calling. This is the default and the recommended value. |
| `react.v1.selfcall` | Uses a ReAct-style interpreter that runs on the same model as the gateway. |

Any other value makes requests to the gateway fail.

## How `react.v1.selfcall` works

On every generation in which tools are available, the interpreter runs before the main generation:

1. AIVAX makes an extra call to the same model with the conversation, the tool definitions as text, and instructions to either pick one tool and its arguments or answer the user.
2. If the model picks a tool, AIVAX converts its text into a tool call and runs it like any other tool call: server-side tools run inside AIVAX, and client-side tools are returned to your application.
3. If the model chooses to answer, the main generation runs without tool definitions.

See [Processing pipeline](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/chat-completions/processing-pipeline.md) for where this step runs.

## Limitations

- **One tool per step.** Parallel tool calls are not possible.
- **More cost and latency.** Every generation with tools adds an extra model call, billed like any other inference.
- **Text-based selection.** Tool names and arguments are parsed from text, so results depend on how well the model follows the interpreter format.

## Migrate away from the interpreter

1. Choose a model with native tool calling that fits the gateway's cost and quality requirements.
2. Change the gateway model and set the tool calling handler to `native`, or remove `knownToolHandlerName`.
3. Test the gateway's tool flows, for example with [Agentic Tests](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/agentic-tests.md), before switching production traffic.

---

Source: https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/chat-completions/limits.html

# Inference limits

This page lists the limits that apply to `chat/completions` requests. Account-wide request rates and plan limits are documented in [Plans and limits](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/limits.md).

## Rate limits

Requests count toward the account's plan limits for integrated models or BYOK, and return `429 Too Many Requests` when a limit is reached. Requests to subscription models also return `429` when the plan's monthly subscription model quota is exhausted. See [Plans and limits](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/limits.md).

## Context window

The context window is the model's maximum input size. A gateway can set a lower limit with `contextMaximumSize` and choose what happens when a conversation exceeds it; see [Context truncation](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/chat-completions/context-truncation.md).

On the Free plan, the input context is capped at 64,000 tokens, even when the model or the gateway allows more.

## Remote instruction sources

Each remote instruction source response can be at most 5 MB. See [Processing pipeline](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/chat-completions/processing-pipeline.md#instructions).

## Output length

`max_completion_tokens` limits the generated output. `max_tokens` is accepted as an alias. When omitted, the model's default applies.

## Conversation token

- `conversation_token` accepts any non-empty string with 128 characters or less.
- Server-side tool state is kept for one hour after its last use.
- `idempotency_key` is a deprecated alias of `conversation_token`.

See [Session reuse](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/chat-completions/session-reuse.md).

## Structured output

JSON Healing makes 3 attempts by default. `healing_options.max_attempts` accepts 1 to 10. See [JSON Healing](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/structured-responses/json-healing.md).

## Media

- Requests with files or videos require a higher minimum account balance than requests with images or audio.
- External media URLs must be reachable without authentication. Provider-specific size limits apply.
- Large videos should be sent by URL instead of base64.

See [Input and multimodality](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/chat-completions/input-and-multimodality.md#media-requirements).

## Request duration

A request can run several generations and tool calls. On `https://inference.aivax.net`, a non-streaming request that exceeds the proxy timeout returns `524`. Use streaming, or send long requests to the direct inference host; see [Long-running inference](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/chat-completions/concepts.md#long-running-inference).

## Public API keys

Public keys are designed for code that runs in a browser. With a public key, `chat/completions`:

- accepts only a gateway's full ID in `model`, not slugs or integrated model names;
- accepts only these request fields: `model`, `messages`, `prompt`, `temperature`, `top_p`, `top_k`, `seed`, `tools`, `reasoning_effort`, `max_completion_tokens`, `stream`, `conversation_token`, and `idempotency_key`. Any other field returns `400 Bad Request`;
- does not use the gateway's MCP sources, protocol functions, built-in tools, shell, or skills;
- applies request and token rate limits per key and per remote address. See [Public API keys](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/limits.md#public-api-keys) for the values.

See [Authentication](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/authentication.md) before exposing a public key.

---

Source: https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/chat-completions/troubleshooting.html

# Troubleshooting inference

AIVAX uses two response styles:

- OpenAI-compatible endpoints return an OpenAI-style `error` object.
- Account and administrative endpoints return an AIVAX response envelope with an error or a successful `data` value.

| Status | What to check |
| --- | --- |
| `400 Bad Request` | Confirm the model or gateway identifier and remove unsupported parameters from the request. |
| `401 Unauthorized` | Confirm that the private key is present, complete, active, and sent through the SDK configuration. |
| `402 Payment Required` | Review [Pricing](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/pricing.md) and confirm that the account is ready for a billable request. |
| `403 Forbidden` | Confirm that the key type, model, or selected resource allows this operation. |
| `429 Too Many Requests` | Retry later and review [Plans and limits](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/limits.md) before increasing request volume. If the message says the subscription model quota is exhausted, it renews one month after the first request that used it; use another model in the meantime. See [Monthly subscription model quota](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/limits.md#monthly-subscription-model-quota). |
| `500 Internal Server Error` | An unexpected error occurred. Retry later. |
| `503 Service Unavailable` | A service AIVAX depends on is temporarily unavailable. Retry after the interval in the `Retry-After` header. |
| `524` or proxy timeout | The request took longer than the proxy allows while AIVAX was still processing it. Send it to the [direct inference host](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/overview.md#long-running-inference) with a longer client timeout. |

If the request still fails, verify in this order:

1. `base_url` is `https://inference.aivax.net/v1`.
2. The API key is available to your process and is a private key.
3. The selected model or gateway exists and is available to the account.
4. For a gateway, test a plain prompt before adding RAG, tools, media, or structured output so you can isolate configuration problems.

## Errors during streaming

After a stream starts, the HTTP status is already `200`. A failure is reported as a final chunk with `finish_reason: "error"` and an `error` object with `code` and `message`, followed by `[DONE]`. Check for this chunk instead of relying on the status code; see [Streaming](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/chat-completions/streaming.md#errors-during-a-stream).

For integrated models, provider error details are not returned; the message says that the provider is unavailable. For gateways that use your own provider key, the provider's error message is returned as is.

## Common problems

| Symptom | What to check |
| --- | --- |
| The model ignores an image, audio, or file. | The model may not support that modality, or the gateway has `DisableMultiModalInput`. See [Input and multimodality](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/chat-completions/input-and-multimodality.md#when-a-multimodal-request-fails). |
| `Failed to generate a valid JSON response.` | JSON Healing reached its attempt limit. Simplify the schema or the instructions before raising `max_attempts`; see [JSON Healing](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/structured-responses/json-healing.md). |
| The model repeats tool calls from earlier turns. | The request does not reuse the same `conversation_token`, or the state expired. See [Session reuse](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/chat-completions/session-reuse.md). |
| `The 'X' parameter is not allowed with public API keys.` | Public keys accept a reduced set of fields. See [Limits](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/chat-completions/limits.md#public-api-keys). |
| A conversation suddenly fails with a message-size error. | The conversation exceeded the gateway context limit or the Free plan cap. See [Limits](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/chat-completions/limits.md#context-window). |
| A routed request fails although the model exists. | No eligible provider remains after routing, ZDR, or special-provider rules. See [Setup routing](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/routing/setup-routing.md). |

---

Source: https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/routing/setup-routing.html

# Setup provider routing

Some integrated models are available through more than one provider. Provider routing lets AIVAX choose among those providers without changing the model requested by your application. This differs from [model routing](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/ai-gateways/concepts.md#model-routing), which can select a different model based on request complexity.

AIVAX considers providers that are currently available and compatible with the request. If only one provider is eligible, the routing preference does not change the result. When the selected provider fails before it starts answering, AIVAX retries the request on another eligible provider. Provider routing applies only to integrated AIVAX models; a bring-your-own-key gateway uses the provider endpoint configured in that gateway.

You can set routing in three places, from the most general to the most specific: the [AI Gateway](#configure-routing-in-an-ai-gateway), a suffix in the [model name](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/routing/inline-routing.md), and the [request](#override-routing-per-request). Account privacy settings can further restrict the eligible providers; see [ZDR](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/routing/zdr.md) and [Special providers](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/routing/special-providers.md).

Available routing preferences are:

| Preference | Behavior |
|---|---|
| `Balanced` | Balances price, speed, and quality. This is the default. |
| `Cheapest` | Selects the provider with the lowest applicable input and output token price. |
| `Fastest` | Prioritizes the provider with the highest available throughput. |
| `Quality` | Selects the provider that AIVAX ranks highest for quality, without optimizing for price or speed. |
| `Special` | Includes [special providers](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/routing/special-providers.md) and selects the lowest applicable combined input and output token price. |

## Configure routing in an AI Gateway

Use an AI Gateway when the same routing should apply to every request. In the gateway editor, select an integrated model, choose the strategy in **Routing preference**, list provider tags in order in **Allowed providers**, and save the gateway.

The equivalent gateway configuration uses `parameters.routingOption` and `parameters.allowedProviders`:

```json
{
    "name": "Cost-optimized assistant",
    "parameters": {
        "baseAddress": "@integrated",
        "modelName": "YOUR_INTEGRATED_MODEL",
        "routingOption": "Cheapest",
        "allowedProviders": [ "azure-us", "azure-eu", "*" ]
    }
}
```

`allowedProviders` follows the same rules as `routing_options.allowed_providers` below. It defaults to `["*"]`, and an empty list is rejected when saving the gateway.

After saving, call the gateway normally by using its ID or slug as `model`. AIVAX applies the stored routing preference while preserving the gateway's instructions, tools, RAG configuration, and other settings. See [Using an AI Gateway](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/ai-gateways/using-an-ai-gateway.md) for the complete gateway workflow.

## Override routing per request

Use `routing_options` to choose how providers are selected for one request. The override works with a direct integrated model or an AI Gateway that uses an integrated model:

```json
{
    "model": "YOUR_INTEGRATED_MODEL_OR_GATEWAY_ID",
    "messages": [
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": "Summarize this incident report."
        }
    ],
    "routing_options": {
        "preset": "Balanced",
        "allowed_providers": [
            "azure-us",
            "azure-eu",
            "*"
        ]
    }
}
```

| Field | Description |
|---|---|
| `preset` | Routing preference: `Balanced`, `Cheapest`, `Fastest`, `Quality`, or `Special`. When omitted, the gateway's saved `routingOption` is used. |
| `allowed_providers` | Ordered list of provider tags. AIVAX tries the first tag and moves to the next one only when no matching provider is available or compatible with the request. `"*"` matches any provider. When omitted, the gateway's saved `allowedProviders` is used, which defaults to `["*"]`. |

Within each step, `preset` chooses among the matching providers. Without `"*"` at the end, the request fails when none of the listed providers is available. An empty `allowed_providers` list is rejected. Tag matching is case-insensitive.

Each provider's tag is shown in the provider details of the dashboard **Models** page, where it can be copied, and returned as `tag` in the provider list of `GET /v1/models`. A tag identifies a provider endpoint, including its region or variant when one exists, such as `azure-us` or `azure-eu`.

`GET /v1/models` accepts an optional `filter` query parameter with a model name, such as `?filter=@openai/gpt-4o`. The response then contains only that model and its dated snapshots, closest match first. Without `filter`, the full list is returned. See [Deprecated models](#deprecated-models) for how to tell a current model from an old one.

The request values override the gateway's saved routing for that request only; they do not update the gateway. Because `routing_options` is an AIVAX extension, send it as an extra request-body field when using an OpenAI-compatible SDK.

The previous `routing_preset` field is deprecated but still accepted. Replace `"routing_preset": "Fastest"` with `"routing_options": { "preset": "Fastest" }`. When both are sent, `routing_options.preset` takes precedence.

## Provider in responses

Responses for integrated models include a `provider` field next to `model` with the tag of the provider that served the request. In streaming responses, every chunk includes it. The field is `null` for gateways that use your own provider credentials.

```json
{
    "object": "chat.completion.chunk",
    "model": "@openai/gpt-5-mini",
    "provider": "azure-us",
    "choices": [ ... ]
}
```

If a provider fails and AIVAX retries the request on another provider, `provider` reflects the provider that produced the response.

## Deprecated models

Use `_details.provider_model.is_deprecated` in `GET /v1/models` when you need to prefer a current integrated model. It is `true` when the model is flagged as deprecated or was released more than 12 months ago. Deprecated models stay in the list.

A provider can also reroute a retired ID to another model instead of rejecting it, as the Gemini API does for Gemini 2.5 Pro and Flash from December 1st, 2026. See [pinning a model ID versus using an alias](https://aivax.net/blog/pin-llm-model-id-or-use-alias-model-deprecations/).

---

Source: https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/routing/inline-routing.html

# Inline routing in the model name

An integrated model name accepts a routing suffix after `#`. Use it when your client can only change the `model` string, such as an OpenAI-compatible tool or SDK that does not send extra body fields:

| Model name | Effect |
|---|---|
| `@openai/gpt-6-luna#cheapest` | Uses the `Cheapest` preference. Any [routing preference](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/routing/setup-routing.md) works, case-insensitive. |
| `@openai/gpt-6-luna#azure-us` | Uses only the provider with the `azure-us` tag, like `"allowed_providers": [ "azure-us" ]`. |

A suffix that matches a preference name is read as a preference; any other value is read as a provider tag. A provider tag has no `"*"` fallback, so the request fails when that provider is not available. Only one suffix is supported per name.

```json
{
    "model": "@openai/gpt-6-luna#fastest",
    "messages": [
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": "Summarize this incident report."
        }
    ]
}
```

The suffix also works in the model name saved in an AI Gateway and in the model names of the complexity router, so each routed model can have its own routing:

```json
{
    "name": "Cost-optimized assistant",
    "parameters": {
        "baseAddress": "@integrated",
        "modelName": "@openai/gpt-6-luna#cheapest"
    }
}
```

The suffix is resolved at runtime, on every request. It takes precedence over the gateway's saved `routingOption` and `allowedProviders`, but `routing_options` in `chat/completions` stays the final override. For example, `"model": "@openai/gpt-6-luna#cheapest"` with `"routing_options": { "preset": "Quality" }` uses `Quality`. The `model` returned in responses is the model name without the suffix.

---

Source: https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/routing/zdr.html

# Zero data retention providers only

Enable **Zero data retention providers only** in the dashboard account settings to route text inference with integrated models only to providers that declare zero data retention for prompts. Providers that are not classified as zero data retention are excluded before `allowed_providers` and `preset` are applied. When the model has no zero data retention provider available, the request fails instead of falling back to another provider; choose a model with a zero data retention provider or disable the option.

The zero data retention classification is based on the data retention policy each provider declares.

The option applies to text inference. It does not change conversation logging; use `allow_logging` or the account's conversation logging setting for that.

Platform steps that run around a request, such as content moderation, the complexity router, and RAG query rewriting, always use a zero data retention provider, whether or not the account option is enabled. If none is available for one of them, the request fails and can be retried later.

---

Source: https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/routing/special-providers.html

# Special providers

Some integrated models are also offered by special providers, which serve them at discounted prices. Special providers are never selected unless you opt in:

| Routing preference | Special providers |
|---|---|
| `Balanced` | Never used. |
| `Cheapest`, `Fastest`, `Quality` | Considered only when **Allow special providers** is enabled in the dashboard account privacy settings. New accounts allow special providers by default, and the choice can be changed in the welcome dialog or the account settings. |
| `Special` | Always considered, regardless of the account setting. Selects the lowest applicable combined input and output token price among eligible regular and special providers. |

When a model is currently available only through special providers, requests that do not allow them fail. Use the `Special` preference, or enable **Allow special providers** and use a preference other than `Balanced`. [Zero data retention providers only](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/routing/zdr.md) and `allowed_providers` still apply to special providers.

Listing a special provider's tag in `allowed_providers`, or as a `#tag` suffix on the model name, routes to it under any preference, including `Balanced`.

---

Source: https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/structured-responses/concepts.html

# Structured responses concepts

AIVAX can produce structured JSON through two paths:

- `response_schema`: AIVAX validates the final model output against a JSON Schema and retries with validation feedback when the output is invalid. This is the JSON Healing path; [When an LLM returns invalid JSON](https://aivax.net/blog/structured-output-healing-boundary/) explains how truncation, refusals, and repair differ.
- `response_format`: AIVAX passes a native OpenAI-compatible response format to the provider, or applies healing when `healing_options` is present or automatic JSON Healing is enabled on the account.

Use structured responses when another system will consume the output and free-form text would be fragile.

## Choosing a mode

Use `response_schema` when AIVAX should own validation and repair. This is the safest mode for models that do not natively support structured output, for responses that use tools before producing JSON, and for systems that cannot tolerate malformed JSON.

Use `response_format` with `type: "json_schema"` when the provider model should handle the structured output natively. AIVAX will still use the schema internally, and healing is applied when `response_format.json_schema.healing_options` is provided or the account has automatic JSON Healing enabled.

Use `json_only: true` when the HTTP response body should contain only the final JSON. This removes the normal chat completion envelope, choices, usage, and generation metadata from the response body. See [JSON-only](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/structured-responses/json-only.md).

| Page | Covers |
| --- | --- |
| [JSON Healing](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/structured-responses/json-healing.md) | How validation and retries work, native structured output, supported schema features, and failures. |
| [Reasoning and tools](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/structured-responses/reasoning-and-tools.md) | How reasoning models and tool calls combine with a schema. |
| [JSON-only](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/structured-responses/json-only.md) | Returning the bare JSON body, with and without streaming. |

## Long-running structured requests

A structured request can take much longer than a plain one: the model may reason, call tools, and then make several healing attempts, each one a full generation. Without streaming, and always with `json_only`, the client receives nothing until the final JSON is ready, so the request can exceed the proxy timeout of `https://inference.aivax.net` and end with HTTP `524` while AIVAX is still working.

Send these requests to the direct inference host `https://direct.inference.aivax.net/v1` and set a client timeout that covers the expected time, including retries. The request body and the response are the same. See [Long-running inference](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/overview.md#long-running-inference).

For a troubleshooting checklist covering refusals, incomplete streams, and native enforcement versus healing, read [How to fix invalid JSON from an LLM API with structured outputs](https://aivax.net/blog/structured-output-healing-boundary/).

---

Source: https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/structured-responses/json-healing.html

# JSON Healing

JSON Healing is how AIVAX makes any model return JSON that matches a schema, including models without native structured output. Use it when the application must parse a predictable JSON value instead of free text.

Turn it on in one of these ways:

- Send `response_schema`.
- Send `healing_options` in `response_format`.
- Turn on automatic JSON Healing in the account settings.

Use `response_format` when you want the provider's native JSON Schema support. Add `healing_options` inside `response_format.json_schema` when that request should also use JSON Healing.

## How JSON Healing works

When `response_schema` is present, AIVAX follows this loop.

1. AIVAX adds schema instructions to the model request.
2. After the model generates an answer, AIVAX tries to extract JSON from:
   - The complete generated text.
   - JSON code blocks found in the generated text.
3. If the extracted JSON does not validate against the schema, AIVAX adds a feedback message with the validation errors and asks the model to generate the JSON again.
4. This continues until a valid JSON value is generated or the configured attempt limit is reached.

If the model keeps failing the schema, the request fails after the attempt limit; see [When healing fails](#when-healing-fails).

## Basic example

Use `response_schema` when you want JSON Healing on a chat completion, including after tools run. The request below lets the model search the web and then return the results as JSON validated against `response_schema`.

Reference:

[API endpoint reference](https://inference.aivax.net/apidocs?embed=iframe&embed-endpoint=Inference%20(chat%20completions))

<div class="request-item post">
    <span>POST</span>
    <span>
        /v1/chat/completions
    </span>
</div>

```json
{
    "model": "@google/gemini-3.8-flash",
    "prompt": "Search for recent news about electric vehicles.",
    "stream": true,
    "builtin_tools": {
        "tools": [
            "WebSearch"
        ],
        "options": {
            "web_search_mode": "full"
        }
    },
    "response_schema": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
            "news": {
                "type": "array",
                "items": {
                    "type": "object",
                    "properties": {
                        "title": {
                            "type": "string",
                            "description": "News title"
                        },
                        "summary": {
                            "type": "string",
                            "description": "News summary"
                        }
                    },
                    "required": ["title", "summary"]
                }
            }
        },
        "required": ["news"]
    }
}
```

`builtin_tools` is optional. If you enable tools, the selected model must support tool calling or the gateway must provide a tool handler.

## Native structured output

Use `response_format` when you want the provider's native JSON Schema support. If the selected integrated model has strict JSON support, AIVAX can forward the schema using the provider's JSON Schema response format.

```json
{
    "model": "@openai/gpt-4o",
    "messages": [
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": "List 3 European capitals."
        }
    ],
    "response_format": {
        "type": "json_schema",
        "json_schema": {
            "schema": {
                "type": "object",
                "properties": {
                    "capitals": {
                        "type": "array",
                        "items": {
                            "type": "object",
                            "properties": {
                                "city": { "type": "string" },
                                "country": { "type": "string" }
                            },
                            "required": ["city", "country"]
                        }
                    }
                },
                "required": ["capitals"]
            }
        }
    }
}
```

## Enabling healing in `response_format`

Use `healing_options` when the request already uses `response_format` and you also want JSON Healing. Place the options inside `response_format.json_schema`:

```json
{
    "model": "@openai/gpt-4o",
    "messages": [
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": "Return a short status object."
        }
    ],
    "response_format": {
        "type": "json_schema",
        "json_schema": {
            "schema": {
                "type": "object",
                "properties": {
                    "status": { "type": "string" },
                    "message": { "type": "string" }
                },
                "required": ["status", "message"]
            },
            "healing_options": {
                "max_attempts": 5
            }
        }
    }
}
```

`max_attempts` must be between 1 and 10. Each retry is another model generation attempt and can increase cost and latency.

## When healing fails

Healing fails when every attempt produces invalid JSON. The request then fails with the message `Failed to generate a valid JSON response. Please, try again later.`

What the client receives:

- Without streaming, the response is HTTP `503` with the error code `service_unavailable` and the header `Retry-After: 5`.
- With streaming, the stream ends with a chunk whose `finish_reason` is `error` and whose `error` object carries the code and message, followed by `[DONE]`. See [Streaming](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/chat-completions/streaming.md).

If healing frequently reaches the attempt limit, adjust the instruction and schema before raising the limit. Common causes are overly rigid schemas, vague prompts, noisy tool results, or a model that is too small for the task.

## Supported schema features

AIVAX validates the generated JSON with JSON Schema. Supported features:

- `string`: `minLength`, `maxLength`, `pattern`, `format`, and `enum`.
- `number` and `integer`: `minimum`, `maximum`, `exclusiveMinimum`, `exclusiveMaximum`, and `multipleOf`.
- `array`: `items`, `uniqueItems`, `minItems`, and `maxItems`.
- `object`: `properties` and `required`.
- `boolean`.
- `null`.
- Multiple types, for example `"type": ["string", "number"]`.

Apply restrictions this way:

- Use `required` for fields your application must receive.
- Use explicit `items` for arrays.
- Use `enum`, `format`, and length or pattern restrictions when the accepted values are known.

## Practical patterns

Use these patterns when you design the schema, not only when you turn healing on.

### Extraction

Tell the model which fields must be inferred, which fields should be `null` when missing, and which fields must not be invented.

### Classification

Use `enum` for the final label. Add a short `reason` field when humans need to audit the decision.

### Tool-backed JSON

Allow the model to use tools before producing the JSON. Include source fields when the application needs provenance.

### Writes to other systems

For database writes or external API calls, validate the JSON again in your application. AIVAX validates the JSON shape, but your application remains responsible for business rules such as permissions, valid IDs, date ranges, and account-specific constraints.

---

Source: https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/structured-responses/reasoning-and-tools.html

# Reasoning and tools

A structured request can use a reasoning model and tools. The model reasons and calls tools as in any other request, and AIVAX validates the JSON only when the model writes its final answer.

## How the request runs

1. The model receives the messages, the tools, and the schema.
2. It can reason and call tools as many times as it needs. Tool calls and their results are not checked against the schema.
3. When the model answers without calling more tools, AIVAX reads the JSON from that answer and validates it against `response_schema`.
4. If the JSON is missing or invalid, AIVAX sends the validation errors back to the model and asks for a new answer. See [JSON Healing](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/structured-responses/json-healing.md).

Only failed JSON answers count toward `max_attempts`. Tool calls and reasoning do not consume attempts.

## Where the JSON comes from

AIVAX reads the JSON from the final answer content, never from the reasoning. The answer can contain the JSON alone or inside a Markdown code block.

Tell the model to put the JSON in its final answer. A model that writes the result only in its reasoning produces an empty answer, which fails validation.

## Streaming

With `response_schema` and healing, the answer text is not streamed while it is being generated, because a partial or invalid answer could be replaced by a retry. Reasoning, tool call events, and usage are still streamed, so the client can show progress. The validated JSON arrives at the end of the stream.

With `json_only`, the stream carries only the final JSON. See [JSON-only](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/structured-responses/json-only.md).

## Example

```json
{
    "model": "@google/gemini-2.5-flash",
    "messages": [
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": "Find the current population of Lisbon and return it as JSON with the source URL."
        }
    ],
    "reasoning_effort": "low",
    "builtin_tools": {
        "tools": ["WebSearch"]
    },
    "response_schema": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
            "city": { "type": "string" },
            "population": { "type": "integer" },
            "source_url": { "type": "string" }
        },
        "required": ["city", "population", "source_url"]
    }
}
```

The model searches the web first, then writes the final answer. Only that answer must match the schema.

## Recommendations

- Use a model that supports tool calling when the request has tools, or a gateway with a tool handler.
- Add source or evidence fields to the schema when the application needs to know where a value came from.
- Keep tool results short. Long or noisy results make it harder for the model to produce a valid JSON at the end.
- Expect longer requests: reasoning, tool calls, and retries add up. Use the direct inference host for long requests, as described in [Concepts](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/structured-responses/concepts.md#long-running-structured-requests).

---

Source: https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/structured-responses/json-only.html

# JSON-only responses

Set `json_only: true` when the client should receive only the generated JSON:

```json
{
    "model": "@openai/gpt-4o",
    "messages": [
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": "List 3 European capitals."
        }
    ],
    "response_schema": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
            "capitals": {
                "type": "array",
                "items": {
                    "type": "object",
                    "properties": {
                        "city": { "type": "string" },
                        "country": { "type": "string" }
                    },
                    "required": ["city", "country"]
                }
            }
        },
        "required": ["capitals"]
    },
    "json_only": true
}
```

With `stream: false`, the HTTP response body is the final JSON with `Content-Type: application/json`. With `stream: true`, AIVAX sends the complete JSON as one SSE data event and then sends `[DONE]`.

---

Source: https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/response-rendering/chat-presentation-guidance.html

# Chat presentation guidance

A streamed assistant turn can contain reasoning, server-side tool activity, partial answers, and the final answer. This page explains how AIVAX delivers each of them and how to present them in a chat interface. See [Streaming](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/chat-completions/streaming.md) for the event format and [Raw multi-turn example](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/response-rendering/raw-multi-turn-example.md) for a complete response.

## Response rendering mode

Set `rendering_mode: "textual_blocks"` when your client wants AIVAX to place reasoning and server-side tool activity in the same textual response flow that the chat UI already renders. This suits clients that build a single response timeline.

```json
{
    "model": "@openai/gpt-5-mini",
    "messages": [
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": "Search for recent product updates and summarize the important changes."
        }
    ],
    "stream": true,
    "builtin_tools": {
        "tools": ["WebSearch"]
    },
    "rendering_mode": "textual_blocks"
}
```

In this mode, reasoning can be emitted as `<thinking-group>` and `<think>` blocks, assistant-facing text can be emitted as `<assistant-answer>` blocks, and server-side tool markers can appear as tool result elements such as `<div class="tool-result reason" data-tool-name="...">`. Parse these blocks into timeline components, collapsible reasoning sections, answer fragments, or tool status rows; do not concatenate every marker into the final assistant answer.

Clients that do not understand this markup should keep the default rendering mode and handle the structured stream events directly. In the default mode, reasoning arrives through `delta.reasoning`, and server-side tool activity arrives through `servertool` events. Keep events in arrival order so reasoning, tool activity, and the answer stay in one timeline.

## Presentation guidance

During generation, reasoning is useful because it lets the user follow what the model is doing before the final answer exists. The assistant can "speak" while it reasons by emitting user-facing process updates or provisional answer fragments. These updates may be interleaved with reasoning blocks, tool calls, and partial answer content as the response develops.

Once the final assistant answer is generated, that answer becomes the main product of the inference. Collapse reasoning by default after completion so the final answer gets the strongest emphasis, and keep it available for users who want to inspect it.

Tool activity should read as status, not speech: use concise labels such as "Searching", "Opening source", "Running tool", "Finished", or "Failed", and keep each tool invocation grouped as one timeline item even if its state changes over time.

A good visual hierarchy is:

- Assistant answer: highest prominence, normal reading typography, part of the main conversation.
- In-progress reasoning: visible enough to show what the model is doing while the response is being generated.
- Completed reasoning: lower prominence, subdued color or container, collapsed or minimized by default.
- Tool blocks: compact status rows with clear loading, success, and error states.
- Raw details: hidden by default unless the client is a developer, audit, or debugging surface.

Show tool names, states, source labels, or short summaries. Hide raw arguments and large payloads unless the user asks for details or the surface is built for technical inspection.

For accessibility, make every collapsed block keyboard-toggleable, give each status row a readable label, avoid relying on color alone for state, and keep motion subtle. A streaming response should feel stable while it updates: new reasoning or tool rows can appear in order, but existing content should not jump around or force the user to lose their reading position.

---

Source: https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/response-rendering/raw-multi-turn-example.html

# Raw multi-turn example

The example below shows the shape of a streamed response when server-side reasoning is visible to the client, [`tool_invocation_explanations`](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/response-rendering/tool-explanations.md) is enabled, and [`textual_blocks`](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/response-rendering/chat-presentation-guidance.md#response-rendering-mode) is used to keep the response timeline textual. Note the ordering: reasoning, assistant answer fragments, tool activity, more reasoning, and the final answer can all belong to the same assistant turn.

```json
{
    "model": "my-custom-model:abc4",
    "messages": [
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": "Which cheap and fast multimodal models should I use for security camera analysis?"
        }
    ],
    "stream": true,
    "builtin_tools": {
        "tools": ["WebSearch"]
    },
    "tool_invocation_explanations": true,
    "rendering_mode": "textual_blocks",
    "extra_body": {
        "reasoning": {
            "enabled": true
        }
    }
}
```

Raw streamed assistant timeline:

```text
<thinking-group>
<think>
The user is asking for cheap, fast multimodal models for security camera analysis.
I should list available AIVAX models and search the documentation before recommending options.
</think>
</thinking-group>

<assistant-answer>
I will check the available multimodal models and identify the best options for security camera analysis.
</assistant-answer>

<thinking-group>
<div class="tool-result reason" data-tool-name="aivax_list_models"><b>aivax_list_models</b><span>Listing the available models in AIVAX</span></div>

<div class="tool-result reason" data-tool-name="aivax_search_context"><b>aivax_search_context</b><span>Searching documentation about multimodal models and image analysis in AIVAX</span></div>

<think>
The relevant models should support VideoInput or ImageInput, have low input cost, and be fast enough for camera workflows.
I found several candidates and should rank them by cost, speed, and modality support.
</think>
</thinking-group>

<assistant-answer>
For security camera analysis, prioritize models with VideoInput, low input pricing, and high speed.

Model availability and prices change over time; the picks below are example output — see [Pricing](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/pricing.md) for current values.

Top picks:

1. @google/gemini-3.5-flash-lite: fast, inexpensive, and supports video.
2. @qwen/qwen3.5-9b: low input cost in this example output with video support.
3. @amazon/nova-lite: low input cost and a large context window.

Use VideoInput for clips when possible. If a model only supports ImageInput, extract frames from the camera stream before sending them.
</assistant-answer>
```

When the user replies, keep the conversation history focused on the user-visible assistant result. Store reasoning and tool details as timeline or audit metadata if your product needs them, but do not turn them into a new user message. The assistant message should use the content from the final `<assistant-answer>` block, not the full reasoning transcript.

```json
{
    "model": "my-custom-model:abc4",
    "messages": [
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": "Which cheap and fast multimodal models should I use for security camera analysis?"
        },
        {
            "role": "assistant",
            "content": "For security camera analysis, prioritize models with VideoInput, low input pricing, and high speed.\n\nModel availability and prices change over time; the picks below are example output — see [Pricing](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/pricing.md) for current values.\n\nTop picks:\n\n1. @google/gemini-3.5-flash-lite: fast, inexpensive, and supports video.\n2. @qwen/qwen3.5-9b: low input cost in this example output with video support.\n3. @amazon/nova-lite: low input cost and a large context window.\n\nUse VideoInput for clips when possible. If a model only supports ImageInput, extract frames from the camera stream before sending them."
        },
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": "Now recommend one model for real-time alerts and one for deeper review."
        }
    ],
    "stream": true,
    "builtin_tools": {
        "tools": ["WebSearch"]
    },
    "tool_invocation_explanations": true,
    "rendering_mode": "textual_blocks",
    "extra_body": {
        "reasoning": {
            "enabled": true
        }
    }
}
```

---

Source: https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/response-rendering/tool-explanations.html

# Tool explanations

Use tool explanations when your client shows users why a server-side tool is running. The setting can also be stored on an [AI Gateway](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/ai-gateways/concepts.md#tool-explanations) as `toolInvocationExplanations`. Set `tool_invocation_explanations: true` to ask AIVAX to include explanation fields in server-side tool arguments. When the model supplies `_tool_reason` and `_tool_goal`, `servertool.explanation` contains a client-friendly copy:

```json
{
    "model": "@x-ai/grok-4.3",
    "messages": [
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": "What's the weather forecast for today?"
        }
    ],
    "stream": true,
    "builtin_tools": {
        "tools": ["WebSearch"]
    },
    "tool_invocation_explanations": true
}
```

Example stream event:

```json
{
    "choices": [],
    "servertool": {
        "name": "web_search",
        "id": "call-example-id-0",
        "contents": "{\"query\":\"weather forecast today\",\"_tool_reason\":\"Searching for today's weather forecast online\",\"_tool_goal\":\"I need current weather information to answer accurately.\"}",
        "state": "Created",
        "explanation": {
            "reason": "Searching for today's weather forecast online",
            "goal": "I need current weather information to answer accurately."
        }
    },
    "usage": null
}
```

AIVAX removes `_tool_reason` and `_tool_goal` from the arguments before calling an [MCP server](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/tools/mcp.md) tool or a protocol function callback, so these tools receive only the arguments declared in their schema.

`state` is `Created` when the tool call starts, then `Completed` or `Failed` when it ends. All events of one call share the same `id`, so render them as a single status row that changes state. `explanation` is `null` when the model did not supply both fields; fall back to the tool name in that case.

Show `reason` as the status label, such as "Searching for today's weather forecast online". `goal` is useful in an expanded or audit view. Do not show `contents` to end users unless the surface is built for technical inspection, because it contains the raw tool arguments.

---

Source: https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/chat-clients/overview.html

# Chat Clients Overview

A chat client publishes an [AI Gateway](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/ai-gateways/concepts.md) to end users. It gives them a place to talk to the assistant—a hosted web chat, your own application, Telegram, or WhatsApp—while the gateway keeps answering with its model, instructions, tools, and knowledge. Chat clients support text conversation, deep thinking, search, and image sending. Audio features depend on the channel and the client configuration.

## How a chat client works

A chat client is a session layer on top of an AI Gateway. The two have separate jobs:

- **The AI Gateway** defines what the assistant does: model, instructions, tools, RAG, and skills.
- **The chat client** defines how end users reach it: how a conversation is identified, how long it lasts, which limits apply, what the interface looks like, and how messages enter and leave each channel.

Because of this split, one gateway can serve an internal API, a web widget, Telegram, and WhatsApp at the same time. Each channel keeps its own rules for identity, attachments, formatting, commands, and message delivery.

Every conversation is a [session](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/chat-clients/managing-sessions.md). A session stores the message history, the conversation context, and metadata, and it expires after a configured time.

## Choose a channel

| Channel | Use it when | Guide |
|---|---|---|
| Web client | You want to embed the assistant in a website, product, support center, or dashboard, or call it from your own application. | [Web client](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/chat-clients/web-client.md) |
| Telegram | You need a simple bot with users identified by chat and commands that are easy to test. | [Integrations](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/chat-clients/integrations.md) |
| WhatsApp | Your users' main support channel is already the phone, through Z-API, Evolution API, or Kapso. | [Integrations](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/chat-clients/integrations.md) |

The channel should not change what the gateway knows or does. It may still call for adjustments to tone, response length, formatting, and the attachments you accept.

## Create a chat client

Create the chat client, link it to an AI Gateway, then configure its limits, interface, and integrations. You can do this in the dashboard or through the API:

[API endpoint reference](https://inference.aivax.net/apidocs?embed=iframe&embed-endpoint=Create%20Web%20Chat%20Client)

To change an existing client, use **Edit Web Chat Client** in the API reference. Send only the fields you want to update; omitted fields keep their current values.

Options that are durations, such as `messageDebounceInterval`, `maxScheduledIgnoredZone`, and the integrations' `sessionDuration`, are numbers of seconds.

## Limits

Two limits apply to every session of the chat client, on all channels:

| Limit | Default | What happens when it is reached |
|---|---|---|
| `messagesPerHour` | 20 | New messages from that session are rejected until the hour window allows them again. |
| `maxMessages` | 500 | The session can't receive more messages, and the user must start a new conversation. |

In the web client, a rejected message returns an error. In integrations, the user receives a system message in the chat explaining the limit.

Set both deliberately. Values that are too permissive increase cost and exposure to abuse; values that are too strict hurt the user experience.

## Before you go public

- Review the gateway and chat client configuration, and test the channel with a simple message first.
- Keep API keys on your server. End users only receive the session access key or link, never your account credentials. See [Authentication](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/authentication.md) for the boundary between public chat access and API credentials.
- If the gateway uses persistent memory, explain to users what it stores. Memory is separate from session history: it outlives the session and is tied to the session `tag`. See [the memory-poisoning guide](https://aivax.net/blog/persistent-memory-is-a-write-path/) for reviewing stored context and testing its influence across conversations.
- When a channel does not respond as expected, check the linked gateway and the integration configuration, then retry with a simple message before investigating optional features.

## Next steps

- [Managing sessions](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/chat-clients/managing-sessions.md): create sessions, identify users, and choose where to put context.
- [Web client](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/chat-clients/web-client.md): customize and embed the hosted chat, or send prompts from your application.
- [Integrations](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/chat-clients/integrations.md): connect Telegram and WhatsApp.

---

Source: https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/chat-clients/managing-sessions.html

# Managing Chat Client Sessions

A session is one conversation between a chat client and an end user. It stores the message history, the conversation context, metadata, an access key, and an optional `tag` that identifies the user or conversation. Sessions expire after a configured time.

The web client and your application create sessions explicitly through the API. [Integrations](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/chat-clients/integrations.md) create them automatically, one per conversation in the messaging app.

## Create a session

Create a session from your server, with a private API key, when a user starts a conversation. You can give it context for the whole conversation, such as the user's name or location.

[API endpoint reference](https://inference.aivax.net/apidocs?embed=iframe&embed-endpoint=Create%20Web%20Chat%20Session)

The response contains:

- `sessionId`: the session identifier, used to manage it with your API key.
- `accessKey`: the key that authorizes [Send Prompt](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/chat-clients/web-client.md#sending-prompts-from-your-application) and the other public session routes.
- `talkUrl`: the link to the [hosted web chat](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/chat-clients/web-client.md) for this session.

Anyone with the access key or the link can use the session. Give them only to the user who owns the conversation, and keep them out of logs.

`expires` sets the session lifetime in seconds, counted from creation or refresh. It accepts 600 seconds (10 minutes) through 7,776,000 seconds (90 days) and defaults to 3,600 seconds (one hour).

## Identify users with a tag

Without a `tag`, every session is an independent conversation, reachable only through its access key.

With a `tag`, AIVAX reuses the active session for that tag instead of creating a new one. Creating a session again with the same tag returns the same session and keeps its message history, but replaces its context, expiration, and metadata with the new values. This lets a user come back to the widget, or send another message through the same channel, without losing the conversation.

The `tag` also connects the session to other features:

- [Memory](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/tools/builtin-tools.md) needs a stable identifier to know who a saved preference belongs to.
- [Gateway workers](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/workers.md) and [protocol functions](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/tools/protocol-functions.md) receive it as `externalUserId`, to apply rules per user, channel, or external account.
- Integrations use the chat ID or phone number as the tag, to find the right session for each conversation.

Choose a tag that is stable, unique per user or conversation, and not sensitive, such as an internal user ID instead of an email address.

## Conversation token

Each session has a conversation token that groups its exchanges into one stored [conversation](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/chat-completions/concepts.md). AIVAX creates and manages it; you never send it, unlike `conversation_token` in [session reuse](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/chat-completions/session-reuse.md).

The token is renewed when the conversation is cleared, by the web chat reset or by the `/reset` command in [integrations](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/chat-clients/integrations.md#commands). The following messages are then recorded as a new conversation, even though the session and its `tag` stay the same.

You can read the token in the session transcript, and [protocol functions](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/tools/protocol-functions.md) and [MCP tools](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/tools/mcp.md) receive it in their call context. Use it to correlate calls from the same conversation, not as proof of identity or permission.

## Choose where to put context

AIVAX accepts context in three places. All of them are added to the system instructions of the inference, in this order:

| Field | When it applies | Use it for |
|---|---|---|
| `extraContext` (session) | Every inference in the session. | Context for the whole conversation: the channel, the user's name, plan, preferred language, or the product the conversation is about. |
| `contextLocation` (session) | AIVAX fetches the URL before each inference and appends its content after `extraContext`. | Server-controlled context that can change while the conversation goes on, such as the cart, an order status, or the record open in your application. |
| `instructions` ([Send Prompt](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/chat-clients/web-client.md#add-context-for-one-inference)) | That request only, appended after the `contextLocation` content. | Context for that moment, such as a temporary answer format or the item the user just selected. |

None of them is saved to the session history: the model sees the latest version on each request.

Keep `extraContext` stable during the conversation. Each change to it, or to the content returned by `contextLocation`, invalidates the prompt cache for the whole history, which increases latency and input cost on the next request. For information that changes on every request, or that is not text, use the Send Prompt `context` field instead: it goes into the last user message rather than the system instructions, so the cached history before that message is kept. See [Add disposable context to the last user message](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/chat-clients/web-client.md#add-disposable-context-to-the-last-user-message).

The same rule applies to the channel integrations: Telegram and WhatsApp put their fixed channel context, such as formatting rules and the user's display name, in the session `extraContext`.

Do not put secrets, internal tokens, or data the model should not see in any of these fields. They are sent to the model and can influence responses, tools, and workers. Make sure the `contextLocation` URL is reachable by AIVAX; when it can't be loaded, the inference continues without it and a warning is added to the account logs.

## List and end sessions

To review the sessions of a chat client, with their tags, timestamps, and message and token counts, use **List Web Chat Sessions** in the API reference.

To end a session before it expires, use **Delete Web Chat Session**. Its access key and link stop working immediately.

---

Source: https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/chat-clients/web-client.html

# Web Chat Client

The web client is the browser-facing side of a chat client. You can use it in two ways:

- **Hosted web chat:** send the user to the session `talkUrl`, or embed it in an iframe. AIVAX serves the interface, and you customize how it looks and what it accepts.
- **Your own interface:** keep your application's UI and send each message to the session with [Send Prompt](#sending-prompts-from-your-application).

Both start with a [session](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/chat-clients/managing-sessions.md) created by your server.

## Publish the hosted chat

The access key and the link of a session are its credentials, so create sessions on your server and only hand the result to the user's browser:

1. **Create the chat client** once, linked to your AI Gateway. See [Create a chat client](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/chat-clients/overview.md#create-a-chat-client).
2. **Create a session** from your server when a user opens the chat, with your private API key. Send a stable `tag` to continue the user's previous conversation. See [Create a session](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/chat-clients/managing-sessions.md#create-a-session).
3. **Return the `talkUrl`** from the response to the page that shows the chat. Do not return your API key.
4. **Open or embed the link.** Send the user to it, or load it in an iframe:

```html
<iframe
    src="<talk-url>"
    title="Support chat"
    allow="microphone; clipboard-write"
    style="width: 100%; height: 640px; border: 0;">
</iframe>
```

The `microphone` permission is only needed when `Audio` is in `inputModes`. When the session expires, the link stops working: create or refresh the session again with the same `tag` to get a working link that keeps the conversation.

## Customize the hosted chat

Set these options in the chat client configuration:

| Option | What it controls |
|---|---|
| `pageTitle`, `primaryColor`, `logoImageUrl` | Page title, main color, and logo. |
| `helloLabel`, `helloSubLabel`, `textAreaPlaceholder` | Greeting shown before the first message, and the placeholder of the message box. |
| `suggestionButtons` | Buttons with ready-made prompts, each with a `label` and the `prompt` it sends. |
| `languageCode` | Language of the chat interface. |
| `customStyles`, `customScripts` | Your own CSS and JavaScript, added to the hosted page. |
| `showToolCalls` | Shows the reasoning and tool activity blocks in the conversation. When off, the blocks are hidden and only the status line shows what the assistant is doing. On by default. |
| `debug` | Shows diagnostic information for troubleshooting, and enables `/usage` in integrations. Off by default; turn it off again after use. |

## Attachments and audio

`inputModes` selects what users can attach: `Image`, `Document`, and `Audio`. Enable `uploadUnsupportedFiles` to also accept file types that AIVAX cannot read, sent as generic files.

Attached images, files, videos, and audio are processed before inference. They are forwarded as multimodal content when the gateway's model and configuration support them. When a channel cannot pass an attachment on, AIVAX replaces it with a text notice, so the assistant can still reply clearly.

To reply with audio, set `audioSynthesisSource` to the `name` of a text-to-speech model, as listed by **Get Speech Models** in the API reference. The default, `None`, turns audio replies off. Optionally, set `audioSynthesisVoice` and `audioSynthesisInstruction` to choose the voice and how it speaks. Enable `summarizeTextBeforeAudioSynthesis` to read a summary of long answers instead of the full text. Audio replies are available in the hosted web chat only, not in integrations. See [Speech](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/generations/speech.md) for voices and pricing.

## Sending prompts from your application

Use **Send Prompt** when your application needs a response using an existing chat-client session. The session access key authorizes the request; keep it private. The request uses the session history and the associated AI Gateway configuration.

For long-running inference, send `POST /api/v1/public/chat-clients/<access-key>/prompt` to `https://direct.inference.aivax.net`. Configure your HTTP client's timeout for the expected generation duration. The direct domain exposes selected routes, not the entire chat-client API; see [endpoints available on the direct host](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/overview.md#endpoints-available-on-the-direct-host).

[API endpoint reference](https://inference.aivax.net/apidocs?embed=iframe&embed-endpoint=Send%20Prompt)

### Choose the input format

The required `prompt` accepts plain text, one OpenAI-compatible message object, or an ordered array of message objects. Plain text becomes a user message. Use message objects for multimodal content or tool results, and an array when several messages must be supplied together. At least one message must contain content or tool calls.

The response contains `completionText`, `reasoning` when available, `toolCalls` for your application to execute, `usage`, and `createdMessages`. The last field contains only the messages generated during this request, in generation order—not the submitted messages or the previous session history. Its messages use the OpenAI-compatible format and may include tool calls, tool results, reasoning and per-message metadata.

`completionText` is the text of the last assistant message in `createdMessages`: after a tool call, it holds only the final answer. A tool-call-only turn may return an empty `completionText`, so check `toolCalls` to decide whether to continue.

### Decide whether to save the turn

`commit` defaults to `true`: submitted messages and generated messages are saved to the session. Use `commit: false` for a one-off inference against the current history without saving that turn. You still receive the completion and `createdMessages`.

This is not a dry run: inference is still billed and tools can still act. Uncommitted messages stay out of later session history — to continue that branch, resubmit them in an ordered `prompt` array.

### Add context for one inference

Use `instructions` for context that should apply only to the current request, such as a temporary answer format or the item currently selected in your application. It accepts a string or an array of strings; array entries are joined with blank lines. This context is appended to the system instructions after the session's `extraContext` and any context loaded from `contextLocation`.

Unlike session `extraContext`, `instructions` is not saved as session context, even when `commit` is `true`. It is still sent to the model and can influence responses and tools; do not include secrets or data the model should not see. For context that should last the whole conversation, use the session `extraContext` instead; see [Choose where to put context](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/chat-clients/managing-sessions.md#choose-where-to-put-context).

```json
{
    "prompt": "Is this item still available?",
    "instructions": [
        "The user is viewing product SKU 4471.",
        "Answer in one sentence."
    ]
}
```

### Add disposable context to the last user message

Use `context` to give the model material that belongs to the current turn only, such as a screenshot of what the user is looking at, a document they selected, a short audio clip, or text extracted from your application. It accepts:

- a string, which becomes a text part;
- one OpenAI-compatible content part: `text`, `image_url`, `input_audio`, `video_url`, or `file`;
- an array mixing strings and content parts.

The parts are inserted at the beginning of the last user message of the conversation, before the user's own content. When a tool returned media in a previous step, the context still goes into the message written by the user, not the tool output.

The context is disposable: it is never saved to the session history or to the stored conversation, even when `commit` is `true`, and it is not returned in `createdMessages`. Send it again on each request that needs it. Media parts follow the same rules as attachments in `prompt`: they are forwarded as multimodal content or converted to text according to the model and the gateway's multimodal settings, and that processing is billed as usual.

`context` is the cache-friendly way to send changing information. Unlike `extraContext` and `instructions`, it does not change the system instructions, so the cached part of the conversation is kept up to the last user message. Like every other context field, it is sent to the model: do not include secrets or data the model should not see.

Use `context` for information, not for instructions. Because it is part of the user's message, the model treats it as user input: directives such as "ignore previous rules" or "always answer in JSON" may be ignored, or interpreted as a jailbreak attempt and refused. Put behavior rules, answer formats, and other directives in `instructions` or in the session `extraContext`, which are added to the system instructions.

```json
{
    "prompt": "Is this item still available?",
    "context": [
        "The user is viewing product SKU <sku>.",
        {
            "type": "image_url",
            "image_url": { "url": "https://example.com/product.png" }
        }
    ]
}
```

### Stream the response

Set `stream: true` to receive the response as server-sent events instead of one JSON body. Each `data` line is a JSON object with `type` and `data`:

- `text`: a completion text delta in `content`. When `replace` is `true`, replace the text received so far instead of appending.
- `reasoning`: a reasoning delta in `content`, when the model exposes reasoning.
- `tool`: a server-side tool update with `toolName`, `toolId`, `toolArguments`, and `update` (such as `Created` or `Finished`).
- `result`: the final body, with the same fields as the non-streamed response. It is the last event of a successful request.
- `error`: an error that happened after the stream started, with a `message`. It replaces `result`.

Errors detected before the stream starts, such as insufficient balance or an exceeded message limit, are still returned as regular HTTP errors. `commit` works the same way in both modes: the turn is saved before the `result` event is sent.

### Adjust the inference

Use `inferenceOptions` to override some AI Gateway settings for one request. Omitted fields keep the gateway configuration.

- `reasoningEffort`: the reasoning effort, such as `none`, `low`, `medium`, or `high`, when the model supports it.
- `renderingMode`: `default` or `textual_blocks`. With `textual_blocks`, reasoning and server-side tool activity are placed as textual blocks inside the completion text; see [Chat presentation guidance](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/response-rendering/chat-presentation-guidance.md#response-rendering-mode).
- `toolInvocationExplanations`: whether the model must explain why it calls each server-side tool; see [Tool explanations](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/response-rendering/tool-explanations.md).

```json
{
    "prompt": "Find the latest release notes.",
    "stream": true,
    "inferenceOptions": {
        "reasoningEffort": "low",
        "toolInvocationExplanations": true
    }
}
```

### Complete client-side tool calls

1. Configure the desired client-side tool in the AI Gateway, or send it in the request `tools` field, and send a prompt.
2. When `toolCalls` is nonempty, execute the requested function in your application. Each entry exposes `id`, `functionName`, `contents` (JSON-encoded arguments), and `isProtocolFunction`. Validate the arguments and enforce your application's permissions before execution.
3. Send a new prompt with a `role: "tool"` message. Set `tool_call_id` to the returned call's `id`, `name` to its `functionName`, and `content` to the tool result as text. For multiple calls, submit an array of matching result messages.
4. Read the next completion, or repeat if it requests more tools.

With the default `commit: true`, the assistant's tool-call message is already in the session: submit only the tool results, without duplicating that assistant message. If the preceding request used `commit: false`, include the unsaved conversation messages—including the assistant message containing `tool_calls`—before the results. The top-level `toolCalls` entries are not message objects; use the OpenAI-compatible messages in `createdMessages` when reconstructing that exchange.

Use the request `tools` field for client-side tools that apply only to that inference, such as an action available on the screen the user is on. It takes OpenAI-compatible function tools, added to the AI Gateway tools for that request only; they are not saved to the session. They stay visible even when the gateway hides tools without a skill, and their names must not repeat a gateway tool name. Send the same `tools` again in the request that submits the results, so the model can call them again in the next step.

```json
{
    "prompt": "Add this item to my cart.",
    "tools": [
        {
            "type": "function",
            "function": {
                "name": "add_to_cart",
                "description": "Adds the product the user is viewing to the cart.",
                "parameters": {
                    "type": "object",
                    "properties": { "quantity": { "type": "integer" } },
                    "required": [ "quantity" ]
                }
            }
        }
    ]
}
```

For server-side tools, AIVAX executes the tools and continues generation within the same request. `createdMessages` can therefore contain an assistant tool call, its tool result, and the final assistant reply, while top-level `toolCalls` is empty. Do not execute those server-side calls again. The API reference above includes examples for simple completions, client-side calls, submitted client-side results, and multiple messages from server-side calling.

## Other session routes

With the session access key, your application can also use these routes, described in the API reference:

- **Get Session Info** returns the messages and the client configuration, to render the conversation in your own interface.
- **Retry Last Message** removes everything after the last user message, so the user can try again from there.
- **Download Session Transcript** exports the messages, context, metadata, and conversation token as JSON.

---

Source: https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/chat-clients/integrations.html

# Chat Client Integrations

Integrations connect a chat client to messaging apps, so users can talk to the assistant where they already are. AIVAX supports:

- **Telegram**, through a bot created with BotFather.
- **WhatsApp**, through [Z-API](https://www.z-api.io/), [Evolution API](https://doc.evolution-api.com/), or [Kapso](https://kapso.ai/).

The channel only carries the messages. Inference is still performed by the AI Gateway linked to the chat client, under the same [limits](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/chat-clients/overview.md#limits) as any other session.

## How messages flow

1. The provider sends each new message to the integration's [webhook URL](#webhook-urls).
2. AIVAX finds the session for that conversation, or creates one, and adds the message to its history. Media is downloaded and handled like [web client attachments](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/chat-clients/web-client.md#attachments-and-audio).
3. The gateway generates the reply, which AIVAX sends back through the provider.

Each conversation in the app is its own [session](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/chat-clients/managing-sessions.md), identified by the chat or the user's phone number, depending on the provider. Integration sessions last three hours by default. Change `sessionDuration`, in seconds, in the integration settings to keep them longer or shorter. A session that is still in use is extended automatically, so an active conversation does not expire in the middle of an exchange.

On WhatsApp, the assistant writes with WhatsApp formatting, such as `*bold*` and `_italic_`, because Markdown is not converted.

Integrations reply with text and images. Audio replies are available only in the [hosted web chat](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/chat-clients/web-client.md#attachments-and-audio).

## Configure an integration

Set up the integration in the chat client settings in the dashboard, or with **Edit Web Chat Client Integrations** in the API reference. Each update changes one integration, and only the fields you send are replaced. To disconnect a channel, remove its integration with **Delete Web Chat Client Integration**.

The webhook URL appears after the integration is saved for the first time. Then finish the setup on the provider's side, as described below.

### Telegram

1. In Telegram, open [@BotFather](https://t.me/BotFather) and send `/newbot` to create the bot. BotFather replies with the bot token. To get a new token later, use `/token`.
2. In the chat client, open the Telegram integration and paste the token into **Bot token**.
3. Save, then select **Update hooks**. AIVAX registers the webhook with Telegram for you, including a secret token that proves each request came from Telegram. Messages that were waiting before the registration are discarded.

| Field | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `botToken` | Yes | The token returned by BotFather. |
| `sessionDuration` | No | Session lifetime, in seconds. Three hours by default. |

The bot receives text, photos, voice messages and audio, videos, and PDF documents, including captions. Other document types get a reply saying the format is not supported; stickers and other message types are ignored.

Replies use Telegram's rich formatting, so Markdown, tables, and formulas render in the app. In private chats, the reply appears while it is being written. Each user has their own session, including in group chats. In groups, Telegram's privacy mode decides which messages the bot receives; see `/setprivacy` in BotFather.

### Z-API

1. In the [Z-API](https://www.z-api.io/) panel, open **Instances**, connect your WhatsApp number to an instance, and copy its **Instance ID** and **Instance token**.
2. If you enabled the account security token in Z-API's **Security** tab, copy it too.
3. In the chat client, open the Z-API integration, fill in the fields, and save.
4. In the instance webhooks, paste the AIVAX webhook URL into **On receive**. Leave **Notify those sent by me too** unchecked.

| Field | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `instanceId` | Yes | The ID of the Z-API instance connected to WhatsApp. |
| `instanceToken` | Yes | The token of that instance. |
| `clientToken` | No | The account security token, required only if you enabled it in Z-API. |
| `sessionDuration` | No | Session lifetime, in seconds. Three hours by default. |

The assistant receives text, images with their captions, and audio. Other message types, such as documents, videos, stickers, and locations, are ignored without a reply. Messages sent by the connected number itself are ignored.

### Evolution API

1. On your [Evolution API](https://doc.evolution-api.com/) server, create an instance and connect your WhatsApp number to it.
2. In the chat client, open the Evolution API integration and fill in the server URL, the instance name, and the API key. Save.
3. In the instance webhook settings, set the AIVAX webhook URL, enable the `MESSAGES_UPSERT` event, and leave **Webhook by Events** and **Webhook Base64** disabled.

| Field | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `endpointUrl` | Yes | The base URL of your Evolution API server. |
| `instanceName` | Yes | The name of the instance connected to WhatsApp. |
| `apiKey` | Yes | The API key that AIVAX uses to call your server, sent in the `apikey` header. |
| `sessionDuration` | No | Session lifetime, in seconds. Three hours by default. |

Evolution API has the widest support for incoming messages: text, images, audio, videos, PDF documents, and stickers. Other document types get a reply asking the user to resend the content as text, an image, audio, or a PDF. Messages sent by the connected number itself are ignored.

### Kapso
