   - Examples where appropriate
   - Important constraints or limitations

### Best practices

- **Be specific**: Avoid vague instructions. Instead of “be helpful,” say “provide step-by-step explanations with code examples.”
- **Use imperative language**: Start sentences with action verbs (analyze, explain, compare, list).
- **Keep the scope limited**: Each skill should focus on a specific knowledge area or type of task.
- **Test iteratively**: Refine your skills based on how the model responds in practice.
- **Avoid redundancy**: Do not repeat information already present in the base system instructions.

### Skill example

- Name: Code Performance Analysis
- Description: Use when the user asks for performance analysis, optimization, or bottleneck identification in code.
- Instructions:

```markdown
- Analyze the provided code identifying possible performance bottlenecks
- Consider time complexity (Big O) and memory usage
- Suggest specific optimizations with code examples
- Explain the impact of each proposed optimization
- Prioritize readability and maintainability alongside performance
```

## When to use skills?

Skills are most useful when the agent needs specialized behavior only in some conversations.

### Ideal scenarios

**1. Domain-specific expertise**
- Technical terminology specific to an industry
- Compliance with regulations or standards
- Specific methodologies (Scrum, ITIL, SOC 2, etc.)

**2. Tone or style shift**
- Formal vs. casual service
- Technical vs. simplified communication
- Different personas or roles

**3. Complex, structured processes**
- Multi-step workflows
- Analyses that follow specific frameworks
- Document generation with strict formats

**4. Tasks that require extensive context**
- When instructions are too long to include every time
- Knowledge that is only occasionally relevant
- Multiple mutually exclusive rule sets

### When NOT to use skills

- **Permanent instructions**: If instructions should always be active, put them in the base system instructions.
- **Simple tasks**: For direct answers that don’t require special context.
- **General knowledge**: Information the model already knows well does not need to be reinforced via skills.
- **Too few or too many skills**: Aim for 3–10 skills. Less than that, consider using base instructions. More than that can confuse the model.

### Comparison: Skills vs. System Instructions

| Aspect | Skills | System Instructions |
|--------|--------|----------------------|
| When to apply | On demand, when relevant | Always active |
| Ideal size | Can be extensive | Should be concise |
| Context switching | Yes, can alternate | No, fixed |
| Token usage | Economical (only when needed) | Constant |
| Best for | Specialized knowledge | Base agent behavior |

### Implementation tips

- **Start small**: Implement 2–3 skills initially and expand as needed.
- **Monitor usage**: Check that the model is activating skills correctly.
- **Avoid overlap**: Skills with similar descriptions can confuse the model.
- **Test transitions**: Ensure the model switches skills when appropriate.

## Combine skills with RAG and pipelines

Use skills together with [collections](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/rag/collections.md) when the task needs searchable knowledge, and with [pipelines](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/chat-completions/processing-pipeline.md) when it needs event-time policy or message rewriting. For broader background, see the [Prompt Engineering Guide](https://www.promptingguide.ai/), [Building effective agents](https://www.anthropic.com/index/building-effective-agents), and the [AI Gateway Documentation](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/ai-gateways/concepts.md).

---

Source: https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/batch.html

# Batch Processing

Batch runs the same AI workflow over many independent items. It turns a list of inputs into a background queue with fixed instructions, structured output, optional validation, progress tracking, retries, and result export.

Use Batch when dozens, hundreds, or thousands of records need the same reasoning, and each record can be handled on its own. Typical jobs:

- Classify leads.
- Extract fields from text.
- Enrich records.
- Summarize short documents.
- Evaluate responses.
- Moderate content.
- Generate structured data.
- Call built-in tools for each line of a list.

## What Batch solves

Use Batch when you would otherwise build the queue yourself. Processing many items usually needs error handling, retries, JSON validation, and result export. Batch keeps those parts in AIVAX, so you operate the workload instead of assembling the pipeline.

In practice, it gives you:

- **Repeatable processing:** the same instruction, model, and schema are applied to all items.
- **Asynchronous execution:** the work continues in the background, without keeping a request open.
- **Structured output:** each item can be required to return an object compatible with a JSON Schema.
- **Correction and validation:** AIVAX tries to reprocess invalid responses and can run a second validation step.
- **Operation at scale:** jobs can be started, paused, resumed, monitored, filtered, cleaned, resent for retry, and exported.
- **Operational control:** the UI shows progress, failures, confidence, and job events.

## When to use

Use Batch when each item can be processed on its own and does not need to share memory with the others. A typical item is one line for:

- a client;
- a URL;
- a product;
- a ticket;
- a message;
- a short document;
- a contract snippet;
- a raw record.

Batch is a good choice when:

- the same prompt applies to all items;
- you need tabular or JSON results for later consumption;
- response time can be asynchronous;
- you want to track errors and retry only the problematic items;
- you want to use built-in tools, such as web search, for each item;
- you need to measure confidence and success rate per run.

Do **not** use Batch when:

- the conversation must be real-time;
- one item depends on the previous item's response;
- you are indexing documents for RAG;
- the task is purely deterministic and does not require an AI model.

To index searchable knowledge, use [RAG collections](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/rag/collections.md). For a single immediate response to a user, use [inference](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/chat-completions/concepts.md).

## Concepts

Batch is built from a workflow, a job, and items. Save the workflow once, create a job for each workload, and treat every imported row as its own item.

### Workflow

The workflow is the processing recipe. Create it when many jobs should follow the same rule. It defines how future items will be handled:

- title;
- processing instructions;
- model or AI gateway;
- expected result schema;
- enabled built-in tools;
- validation instructions; and
- retry and error-handling behavior.

Changing a workflow affects subsequent jobs and items processed with that configuration. Use separate workflows when the instruction, schema, model, or validation rules change in a significant way.

### Model and routing

Each item is processed by the integrated model or AI Gateway you choose. Set that choice in the workflow **Model** setting. The API uses the same choice as `modelName`.

When the workflow does not use an AI Gateway, Batch routes each item with the `Cheapest` [provider routing preference](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/routing/setup-routing.md), which selects the available provider with the lowest token price for that model.

Create an [AI Gateway](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/ai-gateways/concepts.md) and select it in the workflow when you need a different route or shared gateway setup. A gateway lets you:

- use the `Balanced`, `Fastest`, or `Quality` preference;
- restrict which providers are attempted;
- apply fixed instructions, tools, and RAG configuration to every item.

### Job

A job is one workload created from a workflow. Use it to group the items you want to process together. It keeps that workload's state, events, and metrics while the job is prepared, processed, paused, or completed.

See the embedded API Reference for supported job states.

### Item

An item is one row from the imported list. Each row becomes an independent input sent to the model with the workflow's instructions.

Each item records its processing outcome, output, confidence, and validation details. See the embedded API Reference for supported item states.

## How to use in the console

Use the console when you want to design the workflow, inspect items, and operate the job by hand. In the AIVAX console, go to **Batch**.

### Create a workflow

A workflow is the rule later jobs reuse. In **Workflows**, create one and configure:

1. **Basic:** set a title, the processing instruction, and the JSON Schema of the result.
2. **Behavior:** choose the supported assistant capabilities for the workflow.
3. **Validation:** enable validation when the response needs to be checked against business rules.
4. **Handling:** configure the workflow's error-handling behavior.

Write the instruction as a general rule, not as a single question. The imported item will be the variable input.

Instruction example:

```text
Classify the company provided in the input. Return the likely sector, a short justification, and signals found in the text. If the input does not contain enough information, use sector "Undefined".
```

Schema example:

```json
{
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "sector": { "type": "string" },
    "reason": { "type": "string" },
    "signals": {
      "type": "array",
      "items": { "type": "string" }
    }
  },
  "required": ["sector", "reason", "signals"],
  "additionalProperties": false
}
```

### Create and run a job

A job is the workload for one run. Create it after the workflow exists. New jobs are created in `Paused` state so you can import and inspect the workload before starting processing.

Choose the import mode that matches the source:

- `lines`: reads one uploaded text file and imports each non-empty line as one item.
- `files`: imports each uploaded plain-text file as one item.
- `zip`: imports each plain-text entry in an uploaded ZIP file as one item.
- `text`: imports the submitted text field as a single item.

Lines can be plain text, delimited CSV, URLs, IDs, compact JSON, or any format the instruction knows how to interpret. For structured line-based inputs, prefer JSONL: one JSON object per line.

Example:

```jsonl
{"name":"Company A","description":"B2B auto-parts marketplace"}
{"name":"Company B","description":"Office specializing in employment contracts"}
{"name":"Company C","description":"Regional pharmacy chain"}
```

#### Chat conversation items

An item can also be a whole conversation instead of plain text. Start the item with the `~[chatconversation,` prefix, followed by a JSON array of messages in the [chat completions](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/chat-completions/concepts.md) format:

```text
~[chatconversation,[{"role":"user","content":"My order arrived damaged."},{"role":"assistant","content":"Sorry about that. Can you send a photo?"},{"role":"user","content":"Sent. I want a replacement, not a refund."}]
```

The prefix is case-sensitive, and everything after the comma must be exactly one JSON array. With a chat conversation item:

- Each message has a `role` (`system`, `user`, `assistant`, or `tool`) and a `content`, which is a string or an array of content parts (`text`, `image_url`, `input_audio`, `video_url`, or `file`). Media parts only work with a model or AI Gateway that accepts that media type.
- The messages are sent to the model as a real conversation, not as text inside a single message. The workflow instruction is added after the last message, so write it as a rule to apply to the conversation above, such as "Classify the customer's main request in this conversation."
- Validation, when enabled, receives the same conversation together with the generated result.
- If the text after the prefix is not a JSON array, the item ends as an execution error that explains the expected format. Fix the input and import it again; retrying the same item does not help.

In the `lines` mode, each line is one item, so write each conversation as compact JSON on a single line. One conversation per file works with the `files`, `zip`, and `text` modes, where line breaks inside the JSON are allowed. Items with and without the prefix can be mixed in the same job.

Start the job when the imported list looks right. The job screen lets you monitor:

- overall progress;
- pending, completed, and failed items;
- average confidence;
- job events;
- most recent processed items;
- full item list with filters by state and confidence.

### Operate on failed items

Use this step when the job has errors, refusals, or results you do not trust yet. Filter the list by execution error, validation error, refusal, or low confidence. Then you can:

- retry all errors;
- retry only execution errors;
- retry only validation errors;
- retry completed items with low confidence;
- remove pending, completed, error, or all non-running items;
- open an individual item to review input, output, state, and confidence.

### Export results

Export when the job finishes and you need the rows outside AIVAX. The file is JSONL. Each line contains metadata, the original input, and the output. Import it into a spreadsheet, database, data pipeline, or manual review step.

## How to use via the API

Use the API when Batch should run inside your own system, data pipeline, or automation. Authentication follows the same pattern as the AIVAX API.

The API flow matches the console. Each step is a separate operation:

1. Create the workflow, the reusable recipe.
2. Create a job from that workflow.
3. Import the items.
4. Start the job when the workload looks right.
5. List, retry, clean up, and export items without losing track of individual records.

If you are still deciding whether Batch is the right feature:

- Use Batch for repeated reasoning over independent items.
- Use [RAG collections](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/rag/collections.md) for searchable knowledge that should be retrieved later.
- Use [direct inference](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/chat-completions/concepts.md) for one immediate answer.

### Create workflow

A workflow is the saved processing rule. Create one when future jobs should reuse the same policy, not a one-time prompt for a single record.

Define:

- the instruction;
- the model;
- the output schema;
- validation behavior;
- retries;
- enabled tools.

[API endpoint reference](https://inference.aivax.net/apidocs?embed=iframe&embed-endpoint=Create%20Batch%20Workflow)

### Create job

A job is one concrete workload. Create it when an existing workflow should process a specific list. Jobs are created paused so you can import and inspect items before processing.

[API endpoint reference](https://inference.aivax.net/apidocs?embed=iframe&embed-endpoint=Create%20Batch%20Job)

Import the items next. Leave the job paused until the list looks right.

### Import items

Import is how a source file becomes independent units of work. Do it after the job exists, and choose the mode that matches the source:

- one line per record;
- one file per record;
- one ZIP entry per record;
- one submitted text as a single record.

[API endpoint reference](https://inference.aivax.net/apidocs?embed=iframe&embed-endpoint=Import%20Batch%20Job%20Items)

See the embedded API Reference for supported import modes, fields, and current constraints.

### Start, pause, or finish

These actions change whether the job keeps running. Use them only after the item list is the workload you intend to process.

- **Start** when the item list looks correct.
- **Pause** to investigate errors or adjust the workflow.
- **Finish** when the job should be terminated rather than resumed.

[API endpoint reference](https://inference.aivax.net/apidocs?embed=iframe&embed-endpoint=Edit%20Batch%20Job)

See the embedded API Reference for the supported job states.

### Monitor

Monitoring tells you whether the workflow is healthy enough to leave running. Use the job view for overall state. Use the item list when you need to see where work is stuck, which items failed validation, and which low-confidence results deserve human review.

[API endpoint reference](https://inference.aivax.net/apidocs?embed=iframe&embed-endpoint=View%20Batch%20Job)

List the job's items when you need the row-level view:

[API endpoint reference](https://inference.aivax.net/apidocs?embed=iframe&embed-endpoint=List%20Batch%20Job%20Items)

Use the list endpoint to filter items by state, confidence, or input text. See the embedded API Reference for supported filters.

### Retry and clean

Retry and cleanup are for items you have already inspected. Retry after you understand the failure shape:

- Retry **execution errors** when the provider or request failed.
- Retry **validation errors** when the response can likely be regenerated into the expected shape.
- Retry **low-confidence results** when the item succeeded but deserves another model attempt.

Use a cleanup endpoint when non-running items are no longer useful and should leave the job.

[API endpoint reference](https://inference.aivax.net/apidocs?embed=iframe&embed-endpoint=Retry%20Batch%20Job%20Items)

Use the retry endpoint after reviewing the failure pattern. See the embedded API Reference for supported retry options and resulting job behavior. For the export filter that matches each retry mode, and how provider batch APIs handle expiry, see [expired batch jobs: partial results and retrying only what failed](https://aivax.net/blog/expired-batch-job-recover-partial-results-retry-failed/).

To remove non-running items from the job:

[API endpoint reference](https://inference.aivax.net/apidocs?embed=iframe&embed-endpoint=Remove%20Batch%20Job%20Items)

Use the removal endpoint only for items that are no longer useful. See the embedded API Reference for supported removal options.

### Export

Export is the handoff from AIVAX back into your workflow. Use it after the job finishes, or export a subset when review needs finished items first and errors later.

JSONL fits spreadsheets, databases, queues, and manual audit tools. Each line stays tied to the original input and its generated output.

[API endpoint reference](https://inference.aivax.net/apidocs?embed=iframe&embed-endpoint=Export%20Batch%20Job)

Use the export endpoint when your review or downstream process needs a selected set of completed results. See the embedded API Reference for supported export filters.

## Availability

Review billing and capacity before you process a large workload. Start with [Pricing](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/pricing.md) and the [limits](#limits) below.

## Limits

Limits are the capacity check for a large workload. The number of workflow items processed per day depends on the plan. See [Batch and Agentic Tests limits](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/limits.md#batch-and-agentic-tests).

These import limits apply to every plan:

| Limit | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Files per import request | 1,000 |
| Total import size | 100 MiB/request |
| Single imported file size | 10 MiB |

Batch processing is asynchronous. If quota pauses or fails the job:

1. Wait until the quota window resets, then retry.
2. Or upgrade the account.

For how provider batch APIs such as OpenAI's limit and fail a batch, and how an AIVAX job pauses on a 429 and resumes, see [OpenAI Batch API rate limits and how a managed job handles 429](https://aivax.net/blog/batch-is-an-admission-control-problem-not-a-queue/).

## Best practices

Use these checks before a large run, while you repair failures, and before you hand results to review.

- Test the workflow with a few items before importing a large list.
- Use restrictive schemas with `required` and `additionalProperties: false` when the output will be consumed by a system.
- Include input and output examples in the instruction when the format is ambiguous.
- Prefer one line per item; if you need to send complex objects, use JSONL.
- Keep validation enabled for sensitive tasks such as legal, financial extraction, or data that feeds automations.
- Use `maxRetries` to fix occasional failures, but investigate repeated errors in the prompt or schema.
- Set a low `errorStopThreshold` in new workflows to avoid spending on a batch with a wrong configuration.
- Retry low-confidence items separately. Low confidence does not mean error, but it indicates the response deserves review.
- Export results by state when manual review is needed, e.g., first `finished`, then `errors`.

Source: https://docs.aivax.net/docs/web-foundation/web-search.html

# Web Search

Web Search retrieves current information from the internet for research, fact checking, and answers that need sources beyond the model's training data. Use it to discover relevant pages; use [Fetch and OCR](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/web-foundation/fetch-and-ocr.md) when you already have a URL or need to read a source in more detail.

## Choose how to use Web Search

| Integration | When to use it |
| --- | --- |
| [Built-in tools](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/tools/builtin-tools.md) | Let an AIVAX model decide when to search during inference. Enable `WebSearch` in the gateway or request's `builtin_tools` configuration. |
| [Web utilities MCP](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/mcp-utilities/web-utilities-mcp.md) | Give an MCP-compatible agent, IDE, or automation client access to the `web_search` tool without running an AIVAX model inference. |
| Direct API | Call the search endpoint from your backend when no model or agent is involved — scheduled monitors, dataset enrichment, or pre-fetching context before inference. |

## Search and verify sources

Write a focused query that includes the topic and any relevant date, product version, or location. For several independent questions, use separate searches rather than combining unrelated topics into one query.

For direct API requests, narrow results with `country` (a two-letter country code), `language` (a language code), and `includeDomains` (trusted domains). Set `topn` to request more results (1–25 per direct API request) when recall matters, such as when surveying competing sources; otherwise, keep the default small count. For parameters of the built-in Web Search tool, see its [reference](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/tools/builtin-tools.md).

Search results help locate evidence; they do not guarantee that a source is accurate or current. Check publication dates, prefer primary sources, and fetch the relevant pages before relying on details that a result summary may omit. Keep source links with the answer so readers can verify the claims. For a pipeline that chains search and fetch and keeps the evidence, see [web search API vs. page fetch for LLM research](https://aivax.net/blog/research-is-a-pipeline-search-discovers-fetch-reads/).

Treat retrieved text as external, untrusted content, not as instructions for your agent.

## API reference

For the supported request, response, authentication, and error contract, use the API Reference:

[API endpoint reference](https://inference.aivax.net/apidocs?embed=iframe&embed-endpoint=Search%20the%20web)

## Pricing and limits

Web Search is billed per search. Calls through [Web utilities MCP](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/mcp-utilities/web-utilities-mcp.md) use the same pricing as the corresponding built-in tool and are charged to the authenticated account. Model inference, when used, is billed separately.

| Description | Pricing |
| --- | ---: |
| Web search | **$5/1k searches** |
| X (Twitter) search | **$5/1k searches** |

Direct API requests return 1–25 results per request (`topn`).

Built-in web search and X/Twitter search have daily plan limits, and X/Twitter search is not available on Free; see [Built-in tools and web search limits](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/limits.md#built-in-tools-and-web-search).

---

Source: https://docs.aivax.net/docs/web-foundation/fetch-and-ocr.html

# Fetch and OCR

Fetch and OCR extracts readable text from web pages and supported documents so applications and agents can use their content for summaries, analysis, or knowledge workflows. The Fetch API can also convert the extracted text into structured JSON using a schema you provide. Use [Web Search](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/web-foundation/web-search.md) first if you need to discover sources rather than read a known URL.

Web pages are processed to remove markup and non-content elements. Document extraction and optical character recognition (OCR) make supported non-text content available as text. Review extracted content before relying on it: scan quality, complex layouts, and tables can affect the result. For measured output, processing-unit costs and per-item errors on real pages, PDFs and receipts, see [URL to Markdown API for LLMs, plus scanned PDFs and images](https://aivax.net/blog/fetch-messy-web-to-text/).

## What you can extract

| Content | Supported formats | Extracted content |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Web pages | HTML, XHTML | Readable page content, such as articles, documentation, and product information, with markup and non-content elements removed. JavaScript and CSS are rendered before extraction. |
| Plain text and Markdown | TXT, Markdown | The document's text, including existing Markdown formatting. |
| PDFs | PDF | Text from digital documents and OCR text from scanned pages. Mixed PDFs can combine direct text extraction with OCR where needed. |
| Images containing text | PNG, JPEG, WebP, TIFF, BMP | Recognized text from screenshots, scanned documents, receipts, and other images with legible writing. |
| Word-processing documents | DOC, DOCX, ODT, RTF | Document text converted into a readable textual representation. |
| Presentations | PPT, PPTX, ODP | Textual slide content. |
| Spreadsheets and tabular files | XLSX, ODS, CSV | Cell and row content as text, for downstream reading or analysis. |
| E-books | EPUB | The publication's text. |

For example, you can fetch an online article, read a PDF manual, extract text from a receipt image, or turn a spreadsheet into text for an agent to analyze. Provide a URL that returns the actual page or file, not a sharing page that requires a login. When submitting a data URI through the API, declare the content's correct MIME type.

The result is extracted text, not a pixel-perfect copy of the original document. Do not assume that layout, table structure, charts, or embedded images will be reproduced exactly. Spreadsheet extraction does not execute formulas or macros.

For a worked example that fetches a PDF, extracts its text, and turns it into RAG-ready chunks, see [PDF to Markdown for RAG](https://aivax.net/blog/pdf-to-markdown-for-rag-chunks-jsonl/).

## Fetch API vs. Media Descriptions

Use the **Fetch API to extract existing text**. Use [Media Descriptions](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/data-processing/media-descriptions.md) to **interpret media with AI**, optionally guided by what your application needs to learn from it.

| | Fetch API | Media Descriptions |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Main purpose | Retrieve readable text from pages and documents, using OCR for supported images and scanned PDFs. | Generate descriptions or extract information from images, PDFs, audio, and video using AI. |
| Output | Extracted text, optional schema-guided JSON generated from that text, processing-unit usage, and per-item errors. | Model-generated content focused by your guidance, which can describe visual or audiovisual information beyond the text present in the source. |
| Images and PDFs | Read text, such as the words on a receipt or the paragraphs in a manual. | Describe visual content or interpret a document, such as explaining a diagram or identifying information relevant to a question. |
| Audio and video | Not an audio/video understanding or transcription API. | Analyze audio and video content. For a dedicated speech-to-text workflow, use [Audio Transcriptions](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/generations/audio-transcriptions.md). |
| Billing | Extraction processing units (PUs), with plan-dependent allowances and rates. Optional JSON conversion is billed separately and is not covered by the extraction allowance. | AI usage charges under Media Descriptions pricing; Fetch PU allowances do not replace these charges. |

For a PDF report, choose Fetch when you need its text for indexing or later analysis. Choose Media Descriptions when you need an explanation of its charts or a guided interpretation of the content. For a receipt image, Fetch reads the printed text; Media Descriptions can interpret the receipt according to your extraction guidance.

When you need specific fields as JSON from text, images, or PDFs, rather than the document's full text, use [Extraction](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/data-processing/extraction.md). It reads the fields directly from each document and bills only input tokens, while Fetch converts to JSON from the extracted text as a separate, inference-priced step. Fetch remains the choice for web pages, other document formats, larger files, and workflows that also need the full text.

Verify consequential details against the original source, and compare the billing paths in the pricing section below.

## Choose an integration

| Integration | When to use it |
| --- | --- |
| Fetch API | Your application controls which URLs or inline base64 data URIs to process and needs structured results, processing-unit usage, and per-item errors. |
| [Web utilities MCP](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/mcp-utilities/web-utilities-mcp.md) | An MCP-compatible client needs to read public URLs through `fetch_url`. This tool accepts one to five URLs per call. |
| [Built-in tools](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/tools/builtin-tools.md) | An AIVAX model needs to read a URL during inference. Enable `OpenUrl` and follow the URL Context configuration guide. |

The integrations have different input contracts. In particular, the MCP tool accepts public URLs; use the Fetch API for inline base64 data URIs. For a backend pipeline that chains search and fetch and keeps an evidence record, see [web search API for LLM agents](https://aivax.net/blog/research-is-a-pipeline-search-discovers-fetch-reads/).

## Fetch content with the API

Authenticate with an AIVAX API key; see [Authentication](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/authentication.md). Supply a non-empty `contents` array containing URLs or base64 data URIs. Each item is subject to a size limit (see [Pricing and limits](#pricing-and-limits)).

The `system.v1.web.fetch` operation accepts these JSON request fields:

| Field | Type | Required | Behavior |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `contents` | Array of strings | Yes | Non-empty list of URLs or base64 data URIs to extract. |
| `returnErrors` | Boolean | No | Defaults to `true`: includes a result for each failed item. When `false`, failed items are omitted. |
| `responseSchema` | JSON Schema object | No | Converts each item's extracted text into JSON guided by this schema. Omit it or use `null` for text-only extraction. The same schema applies to every item in the batch. |
| `responseSchema.instructions` | String | No | Optional extraction guidance inside the schema, such as which details to select or how to handle missing information. This is an AIVAX extension, not a standard JSON Schema keyword. |

### Extract structured JSON

Provide `responseSchema` when your application needs fields from the source rather than only its text. Describe the expected properties, types, and required fields with JSON Schema. Use property descriptions and optional `responseSchema.instructions` to clarify what to extract. For example, an object schema can request a receipt's merchant, date, and total; the embedded reference includes a complete JSON request example.

JSON conversion runs after text extraction. Successful results retain `extractedText` alongside `extractedObject`, so you can compare the generated fields with the extracted source. Without a schema, no JSON conversion runs.

If extraction or JSON conversion fails, `returnErrors` determines whether the failed item appears in the response. A JSON conversion failure does not return a text-only success.

### Read the results

The response contains a `results` array with these fields:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `index` | Zero-based position in the input `contents` array. Use it to match results to inputs, especially when failed items are omitted. |
| `extractedText` | Readable source text, retained on successful JSON conversion; `null` for a failed item. |
| `extractedObject` | Generated JSON value when `responseSchema` is supplied; otherwise `null`. Also `null` for a failed item. |
| `processingUnits` | PUs for fetching and text/OCR extraction, separate from JSON conversion. |
| `jsonProcessingUnits` | PUs for JSON conversion; `0` when no schema is supplied. |
| `error` | Error message for a failed item when `returnErrors` is `true`; `null` on success. Failed items report both PU fields as `0`. |

[API endpoint reference](https://inference.aivax.net/apidocs?embed=iframe&embed-endpoint=Fetch%20web%20contents)

The embedded reference defines the current request and response contract. Check individual results before passing their text to the next step; a failed extraction is not evidence that the source contains no relevant information.

## Access and extraction limitations

A destination may block automated access or require authentication. Fetching a URL does not bypass access restrictions. Use accessible sources or content you are authorized to submit, and correct invalid or inaccessible inputs before retrying.

Treat extracted text as untrusted source material, not as instructions for your application or agent. Review OCR output and schema-guided JSON for exact numbers, names, or other consequential details against the original.

## Pricing and limits

Fetch and OCR extraction is metered in `processingUnits`. Each extraction is either covered by the daily included allowance or billed at the rates below. See [Included daily subscription allowances](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/limits.md#included-daily-subscription-allowances) for the allowance rules. Each item can be up to 50 MB.

| Description | Pricing |
| --- | ---: |
| Fetch and OCR extraction - Free | Base daily allowance; uncovered items **$0.15/1k PUs** |
| Fetch and OCR extraction - Pro | **8× Free** daily allowance; uncovered items **$0.05/1k PUs** |
| Fetch and OCR extraction - Max | **25× Free** daily allowance; uncovered items **$0.03/1k PUs** |
| Fetch and OCR extraction - Ultimate | **50× Free** daily allowance; uncovered items **$0.02/1k PUs** |
| Fetch JSON conversion (`responseSchema`) | Variable inference-based price per PU; charged separately, with no daily extraction allowance |

Optional JSON conversion is metered separately in `jsonProcessingUnits` and is not priced at the OCR rate. The plan's inference multiplier applies to it. Omitting `responseSchema` or setting it to `null` disables conversion and incurs no JSON conversion charge. Do not add both counts and apply the OCR rate to the total.

Examples, assuming items not covered by the daily allowance:

- Plain text and Markdown consume no PUs.
- An HTML page that takes 2.3 seconds to render consumes 23 PUs: $0.00115 on Pro.
- A scanned PDF reporting `processingUnits: 400` costs $0.06 on Free, $0.02 on Pro, $0.012 on Max, and $0.008 on Ultimate. OCR PUs vary with each document.

[Web utilities MCP](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/mcp-utilities/web-utilities-mcp.md) uses the same pricing as the corresponding built-in tool. Model inference, when used to analyze the extracted content, is billed separately. The Fetch API requires a positive account balance.

---

Source: https://docs.aivax.net/docs/generations/images.html

# Image Generation

Use Image Generation to create images from a text prompt in an application workflow. Typical uses include draft illustrations for editorial review, product mockups, marketing variations for A/B testing, and placeholder art that a designer refines later.

Authenticate requests with an AIVAX API key. See [Authentication](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/authentication.md) for authorization guidance.

## Choose a model

Select an image-generation model available to the authenticated account. Model availability and capabilities can change, so obtain current options from the platform instead of depending on a fixed list in this guide.

When several models are available, compare them by capability:

- **Reference images:** only some models accept `referenceImages`.
- **Variations:** decide how many images you need per prompt; `count` accepts 1 to 4.
- **Wait time:** image requests on some models take a while. For those, send the request to `https://direct.inference.aivax.net` and raise your client timeout, as described in [long-running inference](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/overview.md#long-running-inference).

## Generate an image

Use prompts that state the outcome you need rather than relying on vague visual labels. Include the important details, such as the subject, environment, framing, and any text that must be present. One request can carry a single prompt or an array of prompts. Each prompt generates `count` images, and their URLs come back grouped by input prompt.

Control the output with these optional fields:

- `size`: the image dimensions, either as a `"1024x1024"` string or as `{ "width": 1024, "height": 1024 }`. Each side must be between 64 and 4096 pixels. The default is 1080×1920. The model may adjust the size to a dimension it supports.
- `format`: `png`, `jpeg` or `webp`. When omitted, the image keeps the format produced by the model.
- `quality`: an integer from 1 to 100 that sets the `jpeg` or `webp` encoding quality. It has no effect on `png`. When the image is converted and `quality` is omitted, 90 is used.

Each prompt group returns `images`, the URLs of the delivered images, and `outputs`, one entry per requested image in request order. Each entry has the image `url`, the `cost` charged for it and, when it failed, an `error` message with a `null` URL. The group `cost` is the sum charged for that prompt. A request can succeed with some failed images, so check `outputs`.

Supply up to four HTTP(S) reference images when the selected model supports them and the output must follow an existing subject, style, or composition. References guide the result; they do not guarantee identity preservation, so inspect the output before publishing.

Treat generated assets as drafts and review them for accuracy, brand suitability, and unintended content before release. When the first result is close but not right, iterate by tightening one element at a time — subject detail, composition, style constraint — rather than rewriting the whole prompt at once.

The embedded reference is the source of truth for the request shape, supported options, and response fields.

[API endpoint reference](https://inference.aivax.net/apidocs?embed=iframe&embed-endpoint=Generate%20images)

To let an MCP-compatible agent or IDE generate images without calling this endpoint directly, use the [Media generation MCP](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/mcp-utilities/media-generation-mcp.md). For a Claude Code setup, see [generate images in Claude Code with an MCP server](https://aivax.net/blog/generate-images-and-speech-from-claude-code-with-mcp/).

## Pricing, limits, and errors

Image generation is charged per delivered image, with an additional charge per reference image on some models. Failed or undelivered outputs are not charged. Prompt processing is included, and no account or plan multiplier applies. Current tariffs for each model are listed in the Models catalog.

The built-in image generation and editing tool has a daily limit that depends on the plan; see [Built-in tools and web search limits](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/limits.md#built-in-tools-and-web-search).

If a request fails, revise the reported validation issue before retrying.

---

Source: https://docs.aivax.net/docs/generations/speech.html

# Text-to-Speech (TTS)

Use Speech Generation when your application already has final text and needs playable audio without running a chat completion. Typical uses include narrating an article or notification, voicing an IVR prompt, producing a draft voice-over for review, or generating audio files for offline playback.

Authenticate requests with an AIVAX API key. See [Authentication](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/authentication.md) for authorization guidance.

## Choose the delivery form

The endpoint can return audio in two forms, and the right choice depends on the consumer:

- **Binary audio (`raw: true`)** — the response body is the audio file itself, served inline with its MIME type. Use this when a player, browser `<audio>` element, or download flow consumes the response directly.
- **Base64 in the JSON envelope (`raw: false`)** — the response contains the format, MIME type, and base64-encoded audio inside the standard envelope. Use this when the result travels through JSON pipelines, gets stored in a database, or needs to be inspected alongside billing metadata.

Supported formats are `mp3`, `wav`, and `ogg`. When the consumer accepts any of them, prefer `mp3` for smaller payloads and `wav` for maximum compatibility with audio tooling.

## Generate speech

Write text that is ready to be spoken aloud, including punctuation and formatting that communicate pauses or emphasis. Expand abbreviations and numerals the way they should be heard, such as "doctor" instead of "Dr." or "twenty twenty-six" instead of "2026", rather than trusting the voice to guess.

Test the selected voice with representative content before using it in production, especially for names, abbreviations, or specialized terms. Voices differ per speech model, so confirm the voice against the model you will use rather than assuming one model's voices exist in another.

The embedded reference is the source of truth for available models and voices, request options, output formats, and response fields.

[API endpoint reference](https://inference.aivax.net/apidocs?embed=iframe&embed-endpoint=Generate%20speech)

To let an MCP-compatible agent or IDE synthesize speech without calling this endpoint directly, use the [Media generation MCP](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/mcp-utilities/media-generation-mcp.md). It returns a public URL to MP3 audio instead of inline audio.

## Speech or Voice Sessions

Use Speech Generation for one-shot synthesis of known text. Use [Voice Sessions](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/voice-session.md) when the experience is an interactive spoken conversation with interruptions, turn-taking, and tool calls. Chaining transcription, inference, and synthesis manually adds latency that the realtime session avoids.

## Pricing, limits, and errors

Speech generation price varies by model; current tariffs are listed in the [Models catalog](https://aivax.net/models#text-to-speech).

Standalone text-to-speech requests are limited per minute, and per hour on Free; see [Speech limits](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/limits.md#speech). Voice Sessions are not subject to these standalone request quotas; they follow the selected realtime model's access, balance, and inference limits. Review reported validation errors before retrying a failed request.

---

Source: https://docs.aivax.net/docs/generations/audio-transcriptions.html

# Speech-to-Text (STT)

Use Audio Transcriptions to convert recorded speech into text for search, review, captions, or downstream automation. Typical uses include transcribing meetings and interviews, captioning recorded videos, making voice notes searchable, and feeding spoken input into classification or RAG pipelines.

Authenticate requests with an AIVAX API key. See [Authentication](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/authentication.md) for authorization guidance.

## Choose a transcription model

Query the available transcription models for the authenticated account before selecting one. Availability can vary by account configuration, so do not hard-code a catalog in your application.

[API endpoint reference](https://inference.aivax.net/apidocs?embed=iframe&embed-endpoint=Get%20Audio%20Transcription%20Models)

## Transcribe audio

Send the audio as base64 with its format (`wav`, `mp3`, `m4a`, `flac`, `ogg`, `webm`, or `aac`). Decoded audio is subject to the size limit in [Pricing, limits, and errors](#pricing-limits-and-errors). Billing follows the media duration.

Provide the optional `language` hint when the spoken language is known. It steers recognition toward that language and helps with accented speech and domain vocabulary; omit it when the language genuinely varies within one file and let detection handle it.

Review the returned text before using it in user-visible or irreversible actions. The endpoint returns the transcript text without speaker labels.

The embedded reference is the source of truth for accepted request forms, options, and response fields.

[API endpoint reference](https://inference.aivax.net/apidocs?embed=iframe&embed-endpoint=Transcribe%20audio)

## After the transcript

A transcript is usually the start of a pipeline, not the end. Index it into a [RAG collection](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/rag/collections.md) to make recordings searchable, run it through [Batch](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/batch.md) when there are many files, or feed it to [Text classification](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/data-processing/classification.md) to label conversations at scale. For live conversation instead of recorded audio, use [Voice Sessions](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/voice-session.md).

## Pricing, limits, and errors

Transcription price varies by model; current tariffs are listed in the [Models catalog](https://aivax.net/models#speech-to-text).

Standalone audio-transcription requests are limited per minute, and per hour on Free; see [Speech limits](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/limits.md#speech). Transcription requests have a quota separate from speech generation, with the same values. Decoded audio is limited to 75 MB per request. Correct invalid or inaccessible audio before retrying a failed request.

---

Source: https://docs.aivax.net/docs/data-processing/media-descriptions.html

# Media Descriptions

Use Media Descriptions when an application needs structured information from audio, images, video, or PDF content. Typical uses include preparing media for search, moderation review, accessibility workflows, and downstream automation.

Choose the more specialized API when the task is limited to a single medium, such as [Audio Transcriptions](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/generations/audio-transcriptions.md) for speech-to-text.

## Media Descriptions, Extraction, or Fetch

- **Media Descriptions** interprets images, PDFs, audio, and video and returns generated text guided by your instructions. Use it to explain a chart, describe a photo, or answer a question about a video.
- **[Extraction](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/data-processing/extraction.md)** reads text, images, and PDFs and returns the fields defined by your JSON schema, one object per document. Use it when you need the same fields, such as totals or identifiers, from every document. [Summarization](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/data-processing/summarization.md) is its counterpart for short summaries.
- **[Fetch and OCR](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/web-foundation/fetch-and-ocr.md)** returns the readable text of web pages and documents. Use it when you need the full text, for example to index it.

## Describe media or reason over it directly

There are two ways to extract information from media, and they serve different needs:

- **Describe media, then decide** — use this endpoint when you need a reusable text artifact: a description stored for search, a transcript-like record for audit, or input text for a later workflow stage that runs independently.
- **Multimodal inference in one request** — send the media straight to a chat model that supports the input type when the model should reason over it immediately and no intermediate artifact is needed. See [Inference](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/chat-completions/concepts.md).

Prefer Media Descriptions when the extraction guidance is stable and the result feeds several consumers. Prefer direct multimodal inference when the question about the media changes on every request.

## Describe media

Provide media that AIVAX can access, and use guidance that focuses the extraction on the information your workflow needs. The optional `extractionGuidance` instruction narrows the output — "identify the main subject and visible text" for an image, "summarize the sequence of events" for a video — so write it as the question your workflow needs answered.

Results come back in input order. Remote file URLs are downloaded before processing, within a size limit (see [Pricing, limits, and errors](#pricing-limits-and-errors)).

## Choose the engines

The optional `options` object selects the engine that resolves each content type. Omitted engines use `InferenceLow`.

```json
{
    "options": {
        "imageEngine": "InferenceHigh",
        "audioEngine": "Stt",
        "videoEngine": "InferenceLow",
        "fileEngine": "Ocr"
    },
    "input": [ ... ]
}
```

| Field | Accepted values |
| --- | --- |
| `imageEngine` | `InferenceLow`, `InferenceHigh`, `Ocr` |
| `audioEngine` | `InferenceLow`, `InferenceHigh`, `Stt` |
| `videoEngine` | `InferenceLow`, `InferenceHigh` |
| `fileEngine` | `InferenceLow`, `InferenceHigh`, `Ocr` |

- `InferenceLow` describes the content with a smaller, faster, and cheaper multimodal model.
- `InferenceHigh` uses a larger multimodal model that is more accurate and costs more. Use it when small details matter.
- `Ocr` extracts the text of images and files. With `fileEngine: "Ocr"`, any supported document is converted, not only PDFs.
- `Stt` transcribes the speech in audio with a speech-to-text model.

Inference engines return a structured description whose shape depends on the content type. `Ocr` and `Stt` return `{ "textContent": "..." }` and ignore `extractionGuidance`. The engines match those of [Multimodal pre-processing](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/chat-completions/multimodal-pre-processing.md).

The `preset` property is deprecated. It cannot be combined with `options`; a request that sends both is rejected with `400`.

Remote media must be accessible without sign-in. Avoid sending credentials, personal data, or other content that must not appear in a generated description.

The embedded reference is the source of truth for accepted media forms, request options, and response fields.

[API endpoint reference](https://inference.aivax.net/apidocs?embed=iframe&embed-endpoint=Describe%20media)

## Pricing, limits, and errors

| Description | Pricing |
| --- | ---: |
| Media descriptions | **~$1.50/M tokens** |

The price is approximate and depends on the selected engine. `InferenceHigh` costs more than `InferenceLow`; `Ocr` and `Stt` are billed as OCR and speech-to-text usage.

Remote files are limited to 5 MB each. The number of requests per minute depends on the plan; see [Data processing limits](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/limits.md#data-processing).

Correct inaccessible media or invalid content before retrying.

---

Source: https://docs.aivax.net/docs/data-processing/decisions.html

# Semantic Decisions

Semantic decisions evaluate named questions against a shared state and return structured answers rather than a generated explanation. Use them to route support requests, select a category, check a condition, or assign an ordered score.

A request supplies the model, the evidence in `state`, and a `questions` object. Each question has an ID you choose; the response uses the same ID in `answers`. You can ask different question types in one request without making separate API calls.

To evaluate a chat conversation, send it in `input` as an array of OpenAI-style messages instead of `state`. Use one of the two fields, never both. See [Evaluate a conversation](#evaluate-a-conversation).

Use [structured responses](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/structured-responses/concepts.md) instead when you need a larger generated object or a written explanation. For embedding-based similarity between documents and labels, see [Text classification](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/data-processing/classification.md).

## Choose a model

The available decision models, with their aliases, supported question types, context, and prices, are listed in the [Models catalog](https://aivax.net/models#decisions).

Each response returns the canonical model name in `model`. You can also send a model alias, such as `@supersonic-labs/julia:latest`. An alias can move to a newer version when one is released, so pin the canonical name when you need a stable version.

Limits and score interpretation differ between models, so validate a model on representative examples before switching production traffic. For a labeled 40-ticket comparison of four decision models, including how option order changed some answers, see [Gemini Decision 1 vs Jev vs OpenAI Decisions](https://aivax.net/blog/gemini-decision-1-vs-jev-vs-openai-decisions/).

An authenticated API key and a positive account balance are required, including when selecting a model with a zero base token price. See [Authentication](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/authentication.md), [Pricing](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/pricing.md), and [Plans and limits](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/limits.md).

### Discover models programmatically

`GET /api/v1/information/decisions-models.json` lists the current decision-model catalog without authentication. The response's `data` array contains:

- `name`: the canonical identifier to use in a decision request.
- `aliases`: other accepted identifiers for that model.
- `contextLength`: the advertised context in tokens, or `null` when unspecified.
- `maxImages`: the number of images accepted per request, or `0` for text-only models.
- `releaseDate`: the catalog release date in `yyyy-MM-dd` format.
- `capabilities`: question types the model answers (`noul`, `choice`, `score`) and media it accepts (`imageinput`, `audioinput`, `videoinput`, `fileinput`).
- `inputPricePerMillionTokens` and `outputPricePerMillionTokens`: base token prices before account and plan adjustments; see [Usage and cost](#usage-and-cost).

Use this listing to populate model selectors rather than maintaining a separate hardcoded catalog. Model-specific option and question limits are described in [Model-specific limits](#model-specific-limits).

## Write the questions

| Type | `criteria` format | Use it for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `choice` | Object mapping choice IDs to descriptions | Select one destination or category |
| `noul` | Object with nonempty `false` and `true` descriptions | Evaluate a Boolean condition |
| `score` | Ordered array of level descriptions | Evaluate a graded condition |

Every question requires nonempty `instructions`. Use descriptions that distinguish the options, not just opaque IDs. For example, `"billing": "Charges, payments, and refunds"` provides more evidence than `"billing": "B"`.

For `noul`, both criteria are required. Describe what counts as false as carefully as what counts as true, especially when the state might omit the relevant information. For `score`, keep the level order consistent across requests.

## Evaluate a support request

Send the following JSON body to `POST /api/v1/generations/decisions`. The example uses Julia-1; its state may be text, an object, or an array.

```json
{
  "model": "@supersonic-labs/julia-1",
  "state": {
    "message": "I was charged twice. Please return the extra payment."
  },
  "questions": {
    "department": {
      "type": "choice",
      "instructions": "Which team should handle this request?",
      "criteria": {
        "billing": "Charges, payments, and refunds",
        "technical": "Software errors and service outages",
        "sales": "Plans, pricing, and purchases"
      }
    },
    "refund_requested": {
      "type": "noul",
      "instructions": "Does the customer explicitly ask for money back?",
      "criteria": {
        "false": "The customer does not ask for money to be returned",
        "true": "The customer asks for a refund or return of a payment"
      }
    },
    "urgency": {
      "type": "score",
      "instructions": "How urgent is the request based on the stated deadline?",
      "criteria": [
        "No deadline stated",
        "A deadline is stated, but it is not today",
        "The customer explicitly needs resolution today"
      ]
    }
  }
}
```

Tips for reliable answers:

- Keep only relevant evidence in the state.
- Write instructions that explain the decision, not ones that ask for a chain of reasoning or additional text.
- Avoid overlapping choice descriptions unless that ambiguity is intentional.

For one triage request run unchanged on Jev, GPT-6 Luna Decisions and Gemini Decision 1, with routing code and measured cost, see [Jev and OpenAI Decisions API example: triage a support ticket](https://aivax.net/blog/support-triage-typed-decisions/).

### Evaluate a conversation

Use `input` when the evidence is a chat between a customer and an agent, a bot transcript, or any conversation you already store in the [chat completions](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/chat-completions/concepts.md) message format. Send `input` instead of `state`; a request with both returns `400`.

```json
{
  "model": "@supersonic-labs/julia-1",
  "input": [
    { "role": "user", "content": "My order arrived damaged." },
    { "role": "assistant", "content": "Sorry about that. Do you want a refund or a replacement?" },
    { "role": "user", "content": "A replacement, please. I need it before Friday." }
  ],
  "questions": {
    "refund_requested": {
      "type": "noul",
      "instructions": "Does the customer ask for money back?",
      "criteria": {
        "false": "The customer does not ask for money to be returned",
        "true": "The customer asks for a refund or return of a payment"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

- `input` must be a non-empty array. Each message has a `role` (`system`, `user`, `assistant`, or `tool`; `user` when omitted) and a `content` that is a string or an array of content parts.
- Media parts inside messages follow the same formats, capability checks, and image limits as [media sent in `state`](#send-media). A conversation with an image sent to a text-only model returns `400`.
- Long conversations consume more input tokens and count against the model's context limit. Trim messages that do not affect the decision.

### Send media

Some decision models accept media; check `capabilities` and `maxImages` in the [model listing](#discover-models-programmatically). Put each part directly in a top-level `state` array, next to text items written as plain strings. In a conversation, put the same parts in a message's `content` array instead.

| Media | Part | Required capability | Accepted data |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Image | `image_url` | `imageinput` and `maxImages` above zero | Base64 data URL of type `image/png`, `image/jpeg`, or `image/webp` |
| Audio | `input_audio` | `audioinput` | Raw base64 in `data` and a supported `format` |
| Video | `video_url` | `videoinput` | Base64 data URL of type `video/*` |
| Document | `file` | `fileinput` | Base64 data URL or public `https://` URL in `file_data` |

Images use an `image_url` part:

```json
{
  "model": "@cloudflare/clef-omni",
  "state": [
    "Listing title: Red square sticker",
    { "type": "image_url", "image_url": { "url": "data:image/png;base64,<BASE64_IMAGE>" } }
  ],
  "questions": {
    "matches_title": {
      "type": "noul",
      "instructions": "The photo shows the item in the title.",
      "criteria": { "true": "The item in the title is visible", "false": "The item is not visible" }
    }
  }
}
```

- `url` must be a base64 data URL of type `image/png`, `image/jpeg`, or `image/webp`. Remote `http(s)` URLs are rejected.
- Only some models accept images, each up to a per-request maximum. Sending images to any other model, or more than the model accepts, returns `400`. See [Model-specific limits](#model-specific-limits).

#### Audio, video, and documents

Models that list `audioinput`, `videoinput`, or `fileinput`, such as `@google/gemini-decision-1`, accept those parts in the same top-level `state` array. Each part can be combined with text and other media in one request:

```json
{
  "model": "@google/gemini-decision-1",
  "state": [
    "Support call recording and the invoice the customer mentioned.",
    { "type": "input_audio", "input_audio": { "data": "<RAW_BASE64_AUDIO>", "format": "mp3" } },
    { "type": "video_url", "video_url": { "url": "data:video/mp4;base64,<BASE64_VIDEO>" } },
    { "type": "file", "file": { "file_data": "data:application/pdf;base64,<BASE64_PDF>", "filename": "invoice.pdf" } }
  ],
  "questions": {
    "charge_disputed": {
      "type": "noul",
      "instructions": "Does the customer dispute a charge that appears on the invoice?",
      "criteria": { "true": "The customer disputes an invoiced charge", "false": "No invoiced charge is disputed" }
    }
  }
}
```

- **Audio:** `data` is raw base64, without a `data:` prefix. `format` is one of `wav`, `mp3`, `mpeg`, `m4a`, `mp4`, `aac`, `aiff`, `aif`, `flac`, `ogg`, `opus`, or `webm`.
- **Video:** `url` must be a `data:video/...;base64,` URL. Remote video URLs are rejected.
- **Documents:** `file_data` is a base64 data URL, such as `data:application/pdf;base64,...`, or a public `https://` URL. `filename` is optional.
- Sending a part to a model that does not list the matching capability returns `400`.

### Read the response

The success response is a JSON object directly, **without a `data` envelope**. It contains:

- `id`: the decision identifier.
- `model`: the canonical model identifier used for the request.
- `provider`: the provider reported for the result.
- `answers`: an object keyed by your question IDs.
- `usage`: `input_tokens`, `output_tokens`, and the billed `cost`.

For Julia-1, an illustrative `answers` object for the example above is shown below.

```json
{
  "department": {
    "type": "choice",
    "choice": "billing",
    "probabilities": {
      "billing": 0.90,
      "technical": 0.06,
      "sales": 0.04
    }
  },
  "refund_requested": {
    "type": "noul",
    "noul": 0.95,
    "probabilities": {
      "false": 0.05,
      "true": 0.95
    }
  },
  "urgency": {
    "type": "score",
    "score": 0.3,
    "legend": {
      "0": "No deadline stated",
      "1": "A deadline is stated, but it is not today",
      "2": "The customer explicitly needs resolution today"
    },
    "probabilities": {
      "0": 0.8,
      "1": 0.1,
      "2": 0.1
    }
  }
}
```

With Julia-1:

- `choice` is the selected caller-defined ID, not the option description.
- `noul` is the probability assigned to the true criterion, not a JSON Boolean. Your application chooses the threshold and how to handle uncertain cases.
- `score` is the expected **zero-based level index**. In the example, `0 × 0.8 + 1 × 0.1 + 2 × 0.1 = 0.3`. It is not necessarily an integer, and it is not a normalized 0–1 score when there are more than two levels.
- `probabilities` are keyed by choice IDs, `false`/`true`, or score-level indices. `legend` describes the score levels.

Other models may omit optional fields such as `probabilities`, `legend`, or `confidence`, and may use a different score scale. Validate thresholds and escalation rules with labeled examples from your own domain.

## Account rate limits

Semantic decision requests share one per-minute rate limit per account, across all decision models and API keys. Each request counts once, regardless of how many questions it contains. The number of requests per minute depends on the plan; see [Data processing limits](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/limits.md#data-processing).

Requests above the limit return `429 Too Many Requests`. Pace calls across the account and retry with backoff.

## Model-specific limits

These limits apply in addition to the account-level request quota above. Each model's context is listed in the [Models catalog](https://aivax.net/models#decisions).

Most decision models are text-only. The `maxImages` field of the [model listing](#discover-models-programmatically) is the number of images a model accepts per request.

For `@cloudflare/clef` and `@cloudflare/clef-flash`, keep each image under about 300 KB before encoding and the text in `state` under roughly 2,000 tokens.

Julia-1 has these limits:

| Limit | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Questions per request | 1–32 |
| Choices or score levels per question | 2–20 |
| Boolean options | Exactly two: false and true |
| Combined context per question | 1,024 tokens, including state, question, options, and special tokens |
| Question and options budget | 256 tokens within the combined context |
| Description of an individual option | At most 48 tokens |
| Decision payload limit | 256 KiB |

These limits interact: twenty options can exceed the question and options budget even if each description fits its individual limit. Inputs that exceed a limit are rejected, not truncated; shorten descriptions or reduce the option count. The literal `<mask>` is reserved and cannot appear in Julia-1 state, instructions, or option descriptions.

## Usage and cost

Decision models are billed per input token at the base USD rates listed in the [Models catalog](https://aivax.net/models#decisions), before account and plan adjustments (see the [plan multiplier](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/pricing.md#plan-multipliers)).

For Julia-1, the shared state is counted again for each question, so input usage grows with the number of questions. Julia-1 does not generate text, so its `output_tokens` value is zero.

Julia-1 is eligible for the daily semantic decision allowance on every plan, shared across the account. Other decision models are billed normally. See [Plans and Limits](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/limits.md#included-daily-subscription-allowances) for relative plan capacity.

Use the returned `usage.cost` for the billed amount; it is zero when the input is covered by the allowance.

## Errors and reliable use

- **Invalid model or question:** check the model identifier, question type, instructions, and criteria shape. Question IDs and choice IDs must be nonempty.
- **Context or option limit exceeded:** shorten the state or descriptions, reduce the option count, or select a model with suitable limits.
- **Authentication or balance error:** verify the API key and account balance. A zero-priced model still requires a positive balance.
- **Rate limit (429):** reduce the account's request rate and retry with backoff.
- **Temporary unavailability:** retry with backoff and reduced concurrency.

Evaluate `choice`, `noul`, and `score` separately when validating a model, include ambiguous and incomplete states in your test set, and use human review where a wrong decision has material consequences.

## API reference

[API endpoint reference](https://inference.aivax.net/apidocs?embed=iframe&embed-endpoint=Evaluate%20semantic%20decisions)

---

Source: https://docs.aivax.net/docs/data-processing/classification.html

# Text Classification

Use text classification to rank a fixed set of labels for one or more documents without training a custom classifier. It fits tasks such as tagging, triage, or routing requests, where the categories are known in advance and you need a similarity ranking rather than a generated answer.

AIVAX embeds every document and label with the default embedding model and compares their vectors using cosine similarity. For each document, it returns every label ordered from the most similar to the least similar.

Before calling this endpoint, [create an API key](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/authentication.md) and make sure the account has a positive balance.

## Endpoint

<div class="request-item post">
    <span>POST</span>
    <span>/api/v1/generations/classify</span>
</div>

## Request behavior

| Property | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `documents` | `string[]` | Yes | One or more non-empty documents to classify. Results preserve this order and each document's zero-based index. |
| `labels` | `string[]` | Yes | One or more non-empty labels. Every label is scored for every document. |

The endpoint uses the default embedding model and does not accept a model parameter, score threshold, or result limit.

The following request classifies three documents, one of them in German, against three labels:

```json
{
  "documents": [
    "Compare the total cost of two loans for a principal of $10,000 over 5 years at different annual rates",
    "Erklären Sie die Unterschiede zwischen Merge-Sort und Quicksort-Algorithmen in Bezug auf Zeitkomplexität, Platzkomplexität und Leistung in der Praxis.",
    "Write a poem about the beauty of nature and its healing power on the human soul"
  ],
  "labels": [
    "Creative writing",
    "Complex problem",
    "Simple task"
  ]
}
```

## Read the response

`results` contains one item for each input document. Each `scores` array contains every supplied label, ordered by descending cosine similarity. The example below is abbreviated to the first document:

```json
{
  "results": [
    {
      "index": 0,
      "document": "Compare the total cost of two loans for a principal of $10,000 over 5 years at different annual rates",
      "scores": [
        {
          "label": "Complex problem",
          "score": 0.98828
        },
        {
          "label": "Simple task",
          "score": 0.45272
        },
        {
          "label": "Creative writing",
          "score": 0.06823
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

A score measures vector similarity, not a probability. Compare scores within the same request rather than reading a value as a percentage confidence.

## Pricing and limits

| Description | Pricing |
| --- | ---: |
| Text classification | **$0.015/M tokens** |

The number of classified documents per minute and per day depends on the plan; see [Data processing limits](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/limits.md#data-processing). The quota counts every item in the request's `documents` array, not each HTTP request. A request that would exceed any active window returns `429 Too Many Requests`.

The embedded API reference contains the server-maintained request, response, authentication, and error details:

[API endpoint reference](https://inference.aivax.net/apidocs?embed=iframe&embed-endpoint=Classify%20documents)

---

Source: https://docs.aivax.net/docs/data-processing/text-segmentation.html

# Text Segmentation

Text segmentation divides source documents into semantically cohesive strings that can be embedded or indexed in a RAG collection. It returns segments to your application; it does not create embeddings or store submitted documents.

Use it when a source document needs reviewable, retrieval-ready boundaries before you create or update collection documents. If you already have focused, self-contained text, you can import it directly. If you want AIVAX to process source files into collection documents, see [Media Injector](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/rag/documents.md#import-from-files-with-media-injector). For a full walkthrough that turns a PDF into segmented, importable chunks, see [PDF to Markdown for RAG](https://aivax.net/blog/pdf-to-markdown-for-rag-chunks-jsonl/).

To see how segmentation relates to storage, updates, and retrieval, read [where segmentation fits in a RAG pipeline](https://aivax.net/blog/a-vector-database-is-not-a-rag-system/).

## Skip segmentation when the text is already focused

Segmentation earns its keep on long, multi-topic sources — manuals, articles, transcripts — where one embedding per page would blur distinct subjects together. Do not segment text that is already one idea per unit: FAQ answers, product descriptions, short policies, or pre-chunked passages can go straight into the collection. Each unnecessary split adds indexing work and risks separating statements that only make sense together.

## What makes a good segment

A good segment is the smallest span that still answers a question on its own: a complete statement or a tight group of statements about one subtopic, typically a paragraph or a short section. Segments are most useful when the source has clear headings, paragraphs, and complete statements — the segmenter preserves those boundaries instead of cutting mid-thought.

Messy sources, such as tables without headers, OCR output, rambling transcripts, and exports that repeat page headers, benefit from cleaning first. Fix headings and remove boilerplate, then review the results before indexing.

## Prepare source text

Supply complete source text whenever possible, cleaned as described above.

Segments target about 300 tokens and cover the whole document in source order. Boundaries follow the document structure and the meaning of neighboring passages; documents of about that size or smaller are returned as one segment.

Use sanitization only when omitted content is genuinely irrelevant to retrieval. Sanitized requests take longer. When exact source wording or full traceability matters, retain and review the source text instead.

For the supported request, response, authentication, and error contract, use the API Reference:

[API endpoint reference](https://inference.aivax.net/apidocs?embed=iframe&embed-endpoint=Segment%20text)

## Pricing and limits

| Description | Pricing |
| --- | ---: |
| Text segmentation | **$0.10/M tokens** |

The number of segmented documents per minute and per day depends on the plan; see [Data processing limits](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/limits.md#data-processing). The quota counts every item in the request's `documents` array, not each HTTP request. A request that would exceed any active window returns `429 Too Many Requests`.

---

Source: https://docs.aivax.net/docs/data-processing/extraction.html

# Extraction

Use Extraction to turn text, images, and PDFs into JSON shaped by a schema you define. It fits invoices, receipts, forms, contracts, and other documents where your application needs the same fields from every document, such as a number, a company name, a total, or a list of line items.

Before calling this endpoint, [create an API key](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/authentication.md) and make sure the account has a positive balance.

## Extraction, Fetch, or Media Descriptions

These three services read documents, but they return different things:

| | Extraction | [Fetch and OCR](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/web-foundation/fetch-and-ocr.md) | [Media Descriptions](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/data-processing/media-descriptions.md) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Main purpose | Find specific fields in each document and return them as JSON. | Retrieve the readable text of web pages and documents, using OCR when needed. | Interpret media with AI and return a text description guided by your instructions. |
| Input | Text, JPEG, PNG, TIFF, and PDF content. | Web pages and many document formats, including Office files, spreadsheets, and e-books. | Images, PDFs, audio, and video. |
| Output | One JSON object per document, shaped by your schema. | Extracted text, plus optional JSON converted from that text. | Generated text. |
| Billing | Input tokens only. | Processing units with daily plan allowances; JSON conversion is billed separately. | AI usage charges for input and output. |

Choose Extraction when you already know which fields you need and want them read directly from the document. Choose Fetch when you need the document's full text, for example to index it or to read a web page. Choose Media Descriptions when you need an explanation of visual or audiovisual content, such as a chart, a photo, or a video, rather than specific fields.

For a request pattern that keeps a failed document from costing the rest, see [extract structured data from a PDF, one document per request](https://aivax.net/blog/extract-structured-data-from-pdf-llm-api-what-a-failed-batch-costs/).

## Endpoint

<div class="request-item post">
    <span>POST</span>
    <span>/api/v1/generations/extract</span>
</div>

## Build the request

| Property | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `responseSchema` | JSON Schema object | Yes | Object schema whose `properties` describe the fields to extract. It must have at least one property. |
| `documents` | Content part array | Yes | One or more documents as OpenAI-compatible content parts: `text`, `image_url`, or `file`. |
| `instructions` | String | No | Guidance that applies to every document, such as which party counts as the vendor. |

Each property in `responseSchema` is one field to find. Its `description` is the search criterion, so write it as a short, specific definition, such as "total amount due" instead of "total". Nested objects and arrays of objects are supported. `$ref` and `$defs` are not; inline every definition instead.

Images and files accept base64 data URLs or public HTTP(S) URLs:

- Supported formats are JPEG, PNG, TIFF, and PDF, including multi-page PDFs.
- The resource must be reachable without sign-in.
- Other content types, such as audio or video, return `400 Bad Request`.

The following request extracts invoice fields from a text document and a PDF:

```json
{
  "instructions": "Only consider the issuing company as the vendor.",
  "responseSchema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "invoice_number": { "type": "string", "description": "invoice number" },
      "vendor": { "type": "string", "description": "company that issued the invoice" },
      "total": { "type": "number", "description": "total amount due" },
      "line_items": {
        "type": "array",
        "items": {
          "type": "object",
          "properties": {
            "product": { "type": "string", "description": "product name" },
            "quantity": { "type": "integer", "description": "number of units" }
          }
        }
      }
    }
  },
  "documents": [
    {
      "type": "text",
      "text": "Invoice 1042 from Acme Corp. 2 x Widget at $10.00. Total: 20.00 USD."
    },
    {
      "type": "file",
      "file": {
        "filename": "invoice.pdf",
        "file_data": "https://example.com/invoice.pdf"
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

## Read the response

`data` contains one object per document, in the same order as `documents`. Each object uses the property names from your schema. A field that is not found is `null`, and an array with no matches is empty.

```json
{
  "message": null,
  "data": [
    {
      "invoice_number": "1042",
      "vendor": "Acme Corp",
      "total": 20,
      "line_items": [
        { "product": "Widget", "quantity": 2 }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

Documents are processed independently. If any document fails, the whole request returns an error instead of partial results. Documents that finished before the failure are still billed and count toward your quota, so fix or remove the failing document before retrying.

Extracted values are model-generated. Verify consequential values, such as amounts and identifiers, against the original document.

## Pricing and limits

Extraction is billed for the input tokens of each document. Output tokens are not billed.

| Description | Pricing |
| --- | ---: |
| Extraction input | **$0.04/M tokens** |

Extraction and [Summarization](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/data-processing/summarization.md) share the same document limits. Remote files are limited to 5 MB each.
