The number of processed documents per minute and per day depends on the plan; see [Data processing limits](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/limits.md#data-processing).

The quota counts every item in the request's `documents` array, not each HTTP request. A request that would exceed any active window returns `429 Too Many Requests`.

The embedded API reference contains the server-maintained request, response, authentication, and error details:

[API endpoint reference](https://inference.aivax.net/apidocs?embed=iframe&embed-endpoint=Extract%20data%20from%20documents)

---

Source: https://docs.aivax.net/docs/data-processing/summarization.html

# Summarization

Use Summarization to condense text, images, and PDFs into short summaries, optionally guided by instructions about format, focus, language, or length. It fits reports, articles, contracts, and scanned documents that need a quick overview before review, search, or a later workflow step.

A summary restates the document in new words without adding information or commentary. To get specific fields as JSON, use [Extraction](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/data-processing/extraction.md) instead. To ask open questions about media or describe visual content, use [Media Descriptions](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/data-processing/media-descriptions.md).

Before calling this endpoint, [create an API key](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/authentication.md) and make sure the account has a positive balance.

## Endpoint

<div class="request-item post">
    <span>POST</span>
    <span>/api/v1/generations/summarize</span>
</div>

## Request behavior

| Property | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `documents` | Content part array | Yes | One or more documents as OpenAI-compatible content parts: `text`, `image_url`, or `file`. |
| `instructions` | String | No | Guidance that applies to every summary, such as format, language, focus, or length. |

Images and files accept base64 data URLs or public HTTP(S) URLs. Supported formats are JPEG, PNG, TIFF, and PDF, including multi-page PDFs. The resource must be reachable without sign-in. Other content types, such as audio or video, return `400 Bad Request`.

```json
{
  "instructions": "Answer in three bullet points, in English.",
  "documents": [
    {
      "type": "file",
      "file": {
        "filename": "bitcoin.pdf",
        "file_data": "https://bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf"
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

## Read the response

`data` contains one summary string per document, in the same order as `documents`. Documents are summarized independently; to get a single summary of several documents, send them as one text document or summarize the individual summaries in a second request.

```json
{
  "message": null,
  "data": [
    "- Proposes a peer-to-peer electronic cash system that works without a trusted third party.\n- Prevents double spending with a proof-of-work chain of timestamped transactions.\n- Stays secure while honest nodes control most of the computing power."
  ]
}
```

If any document fails, the request returns an error instead of partial results. Documents that finished before the failure are still billed and count toward your quota, so fix or remove the failing document before retrying. Summaries are model-generated; verify consequential information against the original document.

## Pricing and limits

Summarization is billed for the input tokens of each document. Output tokens are not billed.

| Description | Pricing |
| --- | ---: |
| Summarization input | **$0.04/M tokens** |

Summarization and [Extraction](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/data-processing/extraction.md) share the same document limits. Remote files are limited to 5 MB each. The number of processed documents per minute and per day depends on the plan; see [Data processing limits](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/limits.md#data-processing).

The quota counts every item in the request's `documents` array, not each HTTP request. A request that would exceed any active window returns `429 Too Many Requests`.

The embedded API reference contains the server-maintained request, response, authentication, and error details:

[API endpoint reference](https://inference.aivax.net/apidocs?embed=iframe&embed-endpoint=Summarize%20documents)

---

Source: https://docs.aivax.net/docs/data-processing/translations.html

# Translations

Use Translations to translate text, the visible text in images, and the speech in audio into any language. It fits product content, support messages, signs and screenshots, and voice notes that need to reach users in another language.

Before calling this endpoint, [create an API key](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/authentication.md) and make sure the account has a positive balance.

## Endpoint

<div class="request-item post">
    <span>POST</span>
    <span>/api/v1/generations/translate</span>
</div>

## Request behavior

| Property | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `toLanguage` | String | Yes | Language to translate into. |
| `fromLanguage` | String | No | Language of the documents. When omitted, it is detected from each document's content. |
| `documents` | Content part array | Yes | One or more documents as OpenAI-compatible content parts: `text`, `image_url`, or `input_audio`. |

Languages are free-form: a name such as `Japanese`, a code such as `pt-BR`, or a variant such as `Spanish (Mexico, informal)`. The same languages apply to every document in the request.

The service returns only the translated content and preserves formatting, Markdown, code, URLs, numbers, and proper names. Content is always treated as text to translate, not as instructions. For images, it translates the visible text; for audio, the spoken content. Other content types, such as files or video, return `400 Bad Request`.

```json
{
  "fromLanguage": "English",
  "toLanguage": "Brazilian Portuguese",
  "documents": [
    {
      "type": "text",
      "text": "Your order has shipped and should arrive within three business days."
    },
    {
      "type": "image_url",
      "image_url": {
        "url": "https://example.com/sign.png"
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

## Read the response

`data` contains one translated string per document, in the same order as `documents`. If any document fails, the request returns an error instead of partial results. Documents that finished before the failure are still billed, so fix or remove the failing document before retrying.

```json
{
  "message": null,
  "data": [
    "Seu pedido foi enviado e deve chegar em até três dias úteis.",
    "Proibido estacionar"
  ]
}
```

Translations are model-generated. Review them before publishing legal, medical, financial, or other consequential content.

## Pricing and limits

Translations are billed in processing units (PUs), covering input and output usage, and the [plan multiplier](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/pricing.md#plan-multipliers) applies.

The number of translation requests per minute and per day depends on the plan; see [Data processing limits](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/limits.md#data-processing). The limit counts HTTP requests, not documents. A request that would exceed any active window returns `429 Too Many Requests`.

The embedded API reference contains the server-maintained request, response, authentication, and error details:

[API endpoint reference](https://inference.aivax.net/apidocs?embed=iframe&embed-endpoint=Translate%20documents)

---

Source: https://docs.aivax.net/docs/data-processing/instruction-refinement.html

# Instruction Refinement

Use Instruction Refinement to review system instructions, prompts, and skills before you ship them to a model. The service checks them against a catalog of prompt engineering guidelines compiled from model vendors' documentation, then returns a score, prioritized problems located in your text, the guidelines behind each problem, and suggested fixes with patches you can preview and apply.

It fits prompt reviews in pull requests, audits of AI gateway instructions and skills, and editors that highlight problems as you write. It reports guideline issues; it does not run your prompt or measure how a model performs with it. To test behavior against real conversations, use [Agentic Tests](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/agentic-tests.md).

Before calling this endpoint, [create an API key](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/authentication.md) and make sure the account has a positive balance.

## Endpoint

<div class="request-item post">
    <span>POST</span>
    <span>/api/v1/generations/instruction-refinement</span>
</div>

## Choose a view

The review runs in one of two views. Each request runs one view and is billed separately, so run both when you want a complete review.

- **`micro`** (default) reviews the wording inside each item: clarity, measurable constraints, structure, examples, emphasis, tool guidance, output format, and similar guidelines. Use it while writing or editing a single prompt.
- **`macro`** reviews how the items work together as one agent. It checks that the agent has a clear purpose and limits of authority, that each behavior lives in a single item responsible for it, that skills can be selected from their descriptions without overlapping or being forced, that the context matches the tools the agent really has, and that it avoids over-specification such as scripted conversations or rules the platform already provides. Use it when you review a whole agent or its skill set.

The macro view needs the related items to judge relationships. Send the base instructions together with the skills, tool descriptions, and knowledge the agent uses; a single item gives it little to compare.

## Request behavior

| Property | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `view` | String | No | `micro` or `macro`. Defaults to `micro`. |
| `purpose` | String | No | What the agent is meant to achieve. When omitted, the review infers it from the instructions and documentation, and the summary says so. |
| `context` | Object array | Yes | One or more context items, reviewed together. |
| `context[].type` | String | Yes | The item type, described below. |
| `context[].title` | String | No | A label for the item, such as a file or skill name. |
| `context[].description` | String | No | A description of the item. For skills, send the description the agent uses to select the skill, so the review can check whether it activates when needed. |
| `context[].content` | String | Yes | The item text. Must not be empty. |

| Type | Use for |
| --- | --- |
| `instruction` | System or developer instructions that are always loaded. |
| `prompt` | A prompt sent in the user turn. |
| `skill` | An instruction bundle the agent loads on demand. |
| `tool` | The definition or description of a tool available to the agent. |
| `knowledge` | Factual reference content available to the agent, such as products, contacts, or policies. |
| `documentation` | Notes for people about the agent. The agent never sees them. |

Send in one request the items that the same agent receives. A guideline can be satisfied by another item, and findings can point out items that conflict with or duplicate each other; reviewing items in separate requests misses those relationships. In the micro view, `knowledge` and `documentation` items are used only as context.

An unknown `view` or `type`, an empty `content`, or an empty `context` array returns `400 Bad Request`.

```json
{
  "view": "macro",
  "purpose": "Answer billing questions and hand refunds to the finance team.",
  "context": [
    {
      "type": "instruction",
      "title": "support-agent.md",
      "content": "You are a support agent.\nNever promise refunds."
    },
    {
      "type": "skill",
      "title": "refunds",
      "description": "Refunds.",
      "content": "Promise a refund when the customer asks for one."
    }
  ]
}
```

## Read the response

`data` contains the review of all items:

| Property | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `overallScore` | Number | Overall quality from `0` to `1`. Scores below `0.4` mean at least one `P0` finding; scores near `1` mean only minor improvements apply. |
| `summary` | String | A short assessment of the context and its most important improvement. |
| `findings` | Object array | The problems found, up to 20. Can be empty when the context has no relevant problems. |
| `suggestedFixes` | Object array | Concrete changes that resolve one or more findings. In the macro view, conflicts and risks come first. |

Each finding has these properties:

| Property | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `id` | Integer | Identifier of the finding, referenced by `suggestedFixes[].refFinding`. |
| `priority` | String | `P0` for problems that can cause an improper or irreversible action, a regulatory or privacy risk, or leave the agent without identity or purpose; `P1` for likely recurring wrong decisions; `P2` for localized quality loss; `P3` for clarity or organization improvements. |
| `title` | String | Short name of the problem. |
| `description` | String | The problem and its effect on the agent. |
| `locations` | Object array | Every item the finding involves, such as both sides of a conflict. Each location has the `contextIndex` of the item in `context` (zero-based) and an `evidenceSpan`. Can be empty when the problem is not tied to an item. |
| `sources` | Object array | Guidelines that support the finding, described below. |

`evidenceSpan` gives the location of the problem in that item's `content` as `fromLine`, `toLine`, `fromColumn`, and `toColumn`, all 1-based and inclusive. It is `null` when the problem is an omission, when it lies in a skill's `description`, or when the cited text could not be located.

Each source has an `id` that identifies the guideline in its catalog, a `number` within its type, a `type`, and `references` with the vendor documentation URLs behind it. `type` reflects the guideline's weight: a `rule` prevents predictable failures, a `practice` reliably improves results, a `tip` is optional and situational, and a `dont` is an anti-pattern to avoid.

Each suggested fix has a `refFinding` array with the finding ids it resolves, a `description` of exactly what to change and in which item, a `patches` array described below, and a `type`:

| Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `modify` | Rewrite the text in place. |
| `remove` | Delete redundant, conflicting, or harmful text. |
| `transfer` | Move the text to another item or type, such as from the instructions into a skill. The description names the destination. |
| `add` | Write content that is missing. The description names the item that should hold it. |

`patches` holds the fix as text changes. Each patch has the `contextIndex` of the item it changes and a `diff` in unified diff format against the `content` you sent for that item. A fix that changes several items, such as a `transfer`, has one patch per item; apply them together.

`patches` is empty when the fix can't be written as a change to the items you sent, for example when it needs a new skill or tool, or facts only you have. Use the `description` in those cases.

Every patch is computed against the original `content`, independently of the other fixes, so two fixes can change the same lines. When a patch no longer applies because an earlier one changed the same text, skip it or request a new review.

`title`, `description`, `summary`, and fix descriptions are written in the language used by most of the analyzed content.

```json
{
  "message": null,
  "data": {
    "overallScore": 0.35,
    "summary": "The instructions and the refunds skill contradict each other about refunds, and the skill description is too vague to be selected reliably.",
    "findings": [
      {
        "id": 1,
        "priority": "P0",
        "title": "Contradictory refund authority",
        "description": "The instructions forbid promising refunds while the skill requires it, so the agent may promise refunds it cannot grant.",
        "locations": [
          {
            "contextIndex": 0,
            "evidenceSpan": { "fromLine": 2, "toLine": 2, "fromColumn": 1, "toColumn": 22 }
          },
          {
            "contextIndex": 1,
            "evidenceSpan": { "fromLine": 1, "toLine": 1, "fromColumn": 1, "toColumn": 48 }
          }
        ],
        "sources": [
          {
            "id": "B.D. 3",
            "number": 3,
            "type": "dont",
            "references": [
              "https://cookbook.openai.com/examples/gpt-5/gpt-5_prompting_guide"
            ]
          }
        ]
      }
    ],
    "suggestedFixes": [
      {
        "refFinding": [ 1 ],
        "type": "modify",
        "description": "In the refunds skill, replace the promise with: \"Explain that the finance team reviews refunds and transfer the request to them.\"",
        "patches": [
          {
            "contextIndex": 1,
            "diff": "--- a/refunds\n+++ b/refunds\n@@ -1,1 +1,1 @@\n-Promise a refund when the customer asks for one.\n\\ No newline at end of file\n+Explain that the finance team reviews refunds and transfer the request to them.\n\\ No newline at end of file\n"
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

Reviews are model-generated. Read each patch before applying it, check removals against your requirements, and confirm that the changed agent still behaves as expected.

## Pricing and limits

Instruction Refinement is billed in processing units (PUs), covering input and output usage, and the [plan multiplier](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/pricing.md#plan-multipliers) applies. Longer context items consume more input.

Instruction Refinement shares the document limits of [Extraction](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/data-processing/extraction.md) and [Summarization](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/data-processing/summarization.md). Each item in the request's `context` array counts as one document, not each HTTP request. The number of processed documents per minute and per day depends on the plan; see [Data processing limits](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/limits.md#data-processing). A request that would exceed any active window returns `429 Too Many Requests`.

The embedded API reference contains the server-maintained request, response, authentication, and error details:

[API endpoint reference](https://inference.aivax.net/apidocs?embed=iframe&embed-endpoint=Refine%20instructions)

---

Source: https://docs.aivax.net/docs/tools/builtin-tools.html

# Built-in Tools

Built-in tools are capabilities maintained by AIVAX, such as web search, URL reading, code execution, memory, and file generation, that you can enable for a model without writing your own callback. You can combine them with your own [protocol functions](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/tools/protocol-functions.md) and [MCP](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/tools/mcp.md) tools.

Some tools have usage charges. See [Pricing and limits](#pricing-and-limits) before enabling them in a production workflow.

The model decides which tool to call and which arguments to send.

## How to Choose and Combine Tools

Enable only the tools your use case needs. Each tool adds a decision for the model, and similar tools enabled together can lead to redundant or poor choices. Start with the smallest set that solves the use case and write clear instructions on when to use each.

Pick each tool by the kind of need it covers:

- `WebSearch`: the answer depends on public, recent, or changing information.
- `OpenUrl`: the user already provided a URL and wants the assistant to analyze that specific content.
- `Code`: calculations, data transformations, and small algorithmic tasks.
- `Request`: the model must call an HTTP API with a specific method, headers, or body.
- `Remember`: only in chat clients or calls with an identifiable user, because memory tools store and retrieve persistent information for that user.

Treat generation tools (image, document, and web page) as output actions. They do more than improve an answer: they create artifacts that are hosted or attached to the conversation. Tell the model when to generate an artifact and when to reply in text. In support, for example, a document fits a quote, proposal, or formal summary; a web page fits a visual report; an image fits creative ideation. When the user only asks for an explanation, plain text is usually enough.

You can enable tools in two places:

- **In the request**, through `builtin_tools`. The calling application chooses the list for each inference. Use this for testing, internal routines, and flows where the application truly needs to choose tools dynamically.
- **In the [AI Gateway](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/ai-gateways/concepts.md)**. The list is centralized and can be combined with skills, workers, MCP, protocol functions, and shell. Prefer the gateway for permanent production policies, because it prevents different clients from enabling different tools without control.

The values in `builtin_tools.tools` are configuration flags such as `WebSearch`, `Code`, and `OpenUrl`. The model sees runtime function names such as `web_search`, `evaluate_code`, and `open_url`. Use runtime function names when configuring skill tool allowlists or shell tool allowlists.

## Current Date and Time

Enable `DateTime` to expose `get_date_time`. This tool takes no arguments and reads the current time when it is called. It returns the date, time, day of the week, time zone, UTC offset, and an ISO 8601 timestamp.

The tool reports the gateway time zone, set in the gateway's `parameters.timeZone` with an IANA identifier. The default is `America/Sao_Paulo`. In the dashboard, edit **Time zone** under **Date and time** in the gateway's **Parameters + Tuning** tab. Scheduling tools and the Bash tool use the same zone.

To use another zone for a single request to `/v1/chat/completions`, send `time_zone`, such as `"time_zone": "Asia/Tokyo"`. Batch workflows use the time zone of the AI Gateway they run on, or `America/Sao_Paulo` when they name a model directly.

Activation via `builtin_tools`:

```json
{
    "tools": ["DateTime"]
}
```

For a saved gateway, include `DateTime` in `parameters.sentinelOptions.enabledFunctions`. For a Batch workflow, use `enabledTools.enabledFunctions`.

Example tool result:

```json
{
    "date": "2026-07-15",
    "time": "09:30:00",
    "day_of_week": "Wednesday",
    "time_zone": "America/Los_Angeles",
    "utc_offset": "-07:00",
    "date_time": "2026-07-15T09:30:00-07:00"
}
```

The date uses `yyyy-MM-dd`, time uses 24-hour `HH:mm:ss`, and weekday names are returned in English.

## Internet Search

Enable `WebSearch` to let the model search the internet for specific or real-time information, such as weather, news, or game results.

You can choose between two search modes in the dashboard:

- **Full**: inserts the entire content of each result into the conversation context.
- **Summarized**: inserts an AI-generated summary of the results.

`Full` can give more precise results but may consume more input tokens. See [Pricing and limits](#pricing-and-limits) before enabling internet search in production.

> [!NOTE]
>
> The `Full` mode is not always available.

Activation via `builtin_tools`:

```json
{
    "tools": [
        "WebSearch"
    ],
    "options": {
        "web_search_max_results": 10,
        "web_search_mode": "full"
    }
}
```

## Code Execution

Enable `Code` to let the model run JavaScript and inspect the result. Use it for mathematical expressions and other problems that are easier to solve with code than with text.

The code runs in a protected JavaScript environment. It is intended for calculations and small transformations, not for file I/O, network access, or importing external scripts.

Activation via `builtin_tools`:

```json
{
    "tools": [
        "Code"
    ],
    "options": {
    }
}
```

## URL Context

Enable `OpenUrl` to let the model read the content of URLs and links provided by the user.

The tool sends a simple `GET` request to the destination; it does not crawl. Some sites block automated access.

HTML pages are reduced to their plain text, other text is read as is, and files such as documents are converted to text when possible.

Activation via `builtin_tools`:

```json
{
    "tools": [
        "OpenUrl"
    ],
    "options": {
    }
}
```

## Memory

Enable `Remember` when the assistant needs to save information across conversations and retrieve it when relevant. It exposes exactly two tools: `memory_save` and `memory_search`.

Both tools require an identified user: set a stable `tag` in a [chat client](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/chat-clients/managing-sessions.md#identify-users-with-a-tag), or `$.user` in a chat/completions request. Without that identifier, the tools return an error. Memory searches are automatically restricted to the current user. Each memory records the gateway that saved it, and `parameters.builtinFunctionsOptions.allowSharedMemory` controls visibility:

| `allowSharedMemory` | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `true` (default) | The gateway reads, replaces, and deletes the user's memories saved by any gateway in the account. |
| `false` | The gateway only reads, replaces, and deletes the user's memories that it saved itself. |

In the dashboard, this is the **Memory visibility** option in the gateway's tool settings. Memories saved outside a saved gateway are visible only to gateways with shared memory.

Activation via `builtin_tools`:

```json
{
    "tools": [
        "Remember"
    ]
}
```

Memories are **not automatically added to system instructions**. Tell the model when to call `memory_search`, such as before answering a question about a saved preference.

### Save, Replace, or Delete a Memory

`memory_save(id?, content?, expiresInDays?)` combines creation, replacement, and deletion. `id` is the memory's ID; `content` is the text to save, within the memory size limit in [Pricing and limits](#pricing-and-limits); `expiresInDays` is an optional whole number of days, from 1 to 365, after which the memory is deleted automatically.

| Arguments | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `content`, with `id` omitted or `null` | Creates a memory and returns its ID. Without `expiresInDays`, it never expires. |
| `id` and `content` | Replaces that memory's content. Without `expiresInDays`, the current expiration is kept. |
| `id` and `expiresInDays`, with `content` omitted or `null` | Changes only that memory's expiration, counted from now. |
| Only `id` | Deletes that memory. |
| `id` and `content` both omitted or `null` | Returns an error. |

Only memories belonging to the current user can be replaced or deleted. The former `memory_update`, `memory_remove`, and `memory_clear` tools are no longer available; use `memory_save` instead.

### Search Memories

`memory_search(query?, filter?)` requires **exactly one** argument: `query` or `filter`. Sending both, or neither, returns an error.

| Argument | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `query` | A text query for semantic search over the current user's memories. Returns up to 10 results. |
| `filter` | A string using [AIVAX document filter syntax](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/rag/document-filters.md). Returns up to 10 matching memories, newest first. |

Each result contains `id`, `content`, `createdAt`, `updatedAt`, and `expiresAt` (`null` when the memory never expires). Expired memories are never returned. Use `query` to find meaning; use `filter` for exact text, metadata, or creation and update dates:

| Goal | `filter` |
| --- | --- |
| Created in the last 7 days | `createdAt >= now-7d` |
| Changed in the last 24 hours | `updatedAt >= now-24h` |
| Created in October 2026 | `createdAt >= "2026-10-01" and createdAt < "2026-11-01"` |
| Not updated for 90 days, for example stale candidates to review | `updatedAt < now-90d` |
| Mentions a birthday and was created in the last 30 days | `content contains "birthday" and createdAt >= now-30d` |
| Saved in a specific conversation | `metadata.conversation_token = "<conversation token>"` |

For how dates without an offset are interpreted, see [Document filters — Dates](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/rag/document-filters.md#dates).

### Storage and Management

Memories are documents in the `@memories` RAG collection in your AIVAX account. The collection is created automatically on the first save. Each document's content is the memory text, and its metadata identifies the user and originating conversation:

```json
{
    "external_user_id": "<user tag>",
    "conversation_token": "<conversation token>",
    "gateway_id": "<gateway ID>",
    "expires_at": 1791580376
}
```

`gateway_id` is `null` when the memory was not saved by a saved gateway, and `expires_at` is a Unix timestamp in seconds, or `null` when the memory never expires. New or updated memories become searchable within a few seconds.

Expired memories are hidden from `memory_search` and removed automatically. Memories without an expiration are kept until deleted. Inspect and manage memories in the dashboard's Collections and Documents pages or through the [Collections and Documents APIs](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/rag/collections.md). **Deleting the `@memories` collection erases every user's memories in the account**; the collection is recreated on the next save.

The automatic user restriction applies only to the memory tools. When managing the collection directly, use `metadata.external_user_id` to select the intended user's records and preserve the user metadata.

### Billing, Limits, and Errors

Memory has no separate tool charge; see [Pricing and limits](#pricing-and-limits). Both memory tools use the account's [RAG rate limits](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/rag/collections.md#pricing-and-limits). If the account has no balance or reaches a rate limit, the tool returns an error to the model. Instruct the model to report the failure rather than claim it saved or recalled information.

### Migration from Earlier Memory and Calendar Tools

Existing non-expired memories were moved to each account's `@memories` collection, keeping their IDs, user identifiers, creation dates, and expiration dates. Gateways with private memory do not see them, because migrated memories belong to no gateway.

The `Calendar` built-in tool was removed. Requests that still include `Calendar` in `builtin_tools.tools` fail: remove it from your requests. Existing calendar reminders were migrated to text memories.

The former Memories API is no longer available. Move application-level memory management to the Collections and Documents APIs, and update gateway instructions to search explicitly. The former `retentionDays` argument is now `expiresInDays`; omitting it creates a memory that never expires, where the old default was 30 days.

For application-level controls around memory writes, deletion policies, and review, see [How to protect LLM agent memory from poisoning](https://aivax.net/blog/persistent-memory-is-a-write-path/).

## Image Generation

Enable `ImageGeneration` to let the model create images. The available image generation models are listed in the AIVAX console.

Generated images are attached to the conversation context, but the assistant cannot see them directly. They are stored on AIVAX servers for a few months before being permanently removed.

Image generation can incur usage charges. See [Pricing and limits](#pricing-and-limits) before enabling it in production.

You can allow adult images with `image_generation_allow_mature_content`. The selected model must also accept generating such content.

You are always responsible for the [material you generate](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/legal/terms-of-service.md), and it must comply with our terms of service.

Activation via `builtin_tools`:

```json
{
    "tools": [
        "ImageGeneration"
    ],
    "options": {
        "image_generation_model_name": "@x-ai/grok-imagine",
        "image_generation_allow_reference_usage": true,
        "image_generation_quality": "high",
        "image_generation_max_results": 2,
        "image_generation_allow_mature_content": false
    }
}
```

## X Posts Search

Enable `XPostsSearch` to let the model search posts on X (formerly Twitter) and read a specific post when it has the post ID.

It is a direct alternative to [internet search](#internet-search) (`web_search`) for real-time information, such as news or game results, and returns much more recent results. Avoid enabling both tools together, because they serve the same purpose.

This function can incur usage charges. See [Pricing and limits](#pricing-and-limits) before enabling it in production.

Activation via `builtin_tools`:

```json
{
    "tools": [
        "XPostsSearch"
    ],
    "options": {
    }
}
```

## Document Generation

Enable `GenerateDocument` to let the model create PDFs from HTML.

AIVAX hosts the created files and the assistant shares them in the conversation. They are kept for a few months before being permanently deleted.

Activation via `builtin_tools`:

```json
{
    "tools": [
        "GenerateDocument"
    ],
    "options": {
    }
}
```

## Web Page Generation

Enable `GenerateWebPage` to let the model host HTML pages on AIVAX servers, such as reports, landing pages, and infographics.

The pages are kept for a few months before being permanently deleted.

Activation via `builtin_tools`:

```json
{
    "tools": [
        "GenerateWebPage"
    ],
    "options": {
    }
}
```

## Advanced Request

Enable `Request` to give the model a full HTTP request tool. The model can set the method, headers, form fields, and body of each request.

Text responses are returned to the model; binary responses are not, and the tool reports only their content type and size.

Activation via `builtin_tools`:

```json
{
    "tools": [
        "Request"
    ],
    "options": {
    }
}
```

## Pricing and limits

Web and X searches are billed per search. The [plan multiplier](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/pricing.md#plan-multipliers) applies to token-based charges. Model inference used to invoke a tool is still billed at its regular rate. Image generation is billed at the selected model's rates; see [Image generation](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/generations/images.md).

| Description | Pricing |
| --- | ---: |
| Web search | **$5/1k searches** |
| X (Twitter) search | **$5/1k searches** |
| [Memory](#memory) | Saving or replacing content: document embedding; semantic `query` search: RAG query embedding; `filter` search: no cost |
| Advanced requests | No separate charge |
| Document generation | No separate charge |
| Web page generation | No separate charge |

Web search, X/Twitter search, document and web page generation, image generation and editing, general service actions, and [Bash commands](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/tools/shell.md#pricing-and-limits) have plan limits; see [Built-in tools and web search limits](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/limits.md#built-in-tools-and-web-search). X/Twitter search is not available on Free. General service actions share one daily service-action quota. Each memory's content is limited to 10 KB.

## Tool Diagnosis

Use these checks when a tool is not called, is called too often, or fails.

### The tool is not called

1. Confirm that the tool is enabled in the gateway or in the request's `builtin_tools` field.
2. Check whether the selected model supports function calls, or whether a tool handler is configured for models without native support.
3. Review the instructions. If they do not say when to search, open a URL, generate an image, or query memory, the model may answer only from its own knowledge.
4. Test a direct question that clearly requires the tool, such as asking for a recent news article for `WebSearch` or asking to open a specific URL for `OpenUrl`.

### The tool is called too often

Reduce ambiguity. Tools like `WebSearch` and `XPostsSearch` compete for recent information; `OpenUrl` and `Request` can seem similar when the user sends a link. For `Remember`, distinguish a request to save information from a question that requires retrieving an existing memory. Remove unnecessary tools, make gateway instruction descriptions more restrictive, and, when possible, use [workers](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/workers.md) to block or replace calls in specific scenarios.

### The tool fails

Treat tool failures as a normal part of the experience. Searches may return little content, URLs may block bots, APIs may deny authorization, image generation may refuse content, and code execution may receive ambiguous input. Instruct the model to explain the limitation objectively and offer the next step, such as requesting another link, trying a more specific query, asking for authorization, or responding based only on the available context. Do not rely on an external tool as the sole way to conclude a critical conversation without an experience fallback.

---

Source: https://docs.aivax.net/docs/tools/mcp.html

# Support for Model Context Protocol (MCP)

MCP binds external tools to an [AI Gateway](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/ai-gateways/concepts.md). Use it when the assistant must call live services through a standard tool protocol.

The protocol defines tools that run on the server side and enable the assistant to interact with real-time services.

AIVAX acts as an MCP client for gateway inference. For each configured source, it:

1. Connects to the MCP server.
2. Lists tools.
3. Converts each tool schema into a model-callable function.
4. Calls the remote MCP server when the model selects that tool.

<img src="/assets/diagrams/mcp-1.drawio.svg">

## When to use MCP

Use MCP when you already have external tools that need to be discovered and called by models in a standardized way. An MCP server fits:

- Tool catalogs.
- Integrations with internal systems.
- Stateful operations.
- Tools shared among multiple agents.
- Environments where you want to keep logic outside of AIVAX.

Do not use MCP only to replace a single simple HTTP call.

- Use [protocol functions](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/tools/protocol-functions.md) when you need one isolated function with a specific callback and nonce authentication. They are usually simpler.
- Use [built-in tools](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/tools/builtin-tools.md) when the capability already exists in AIVAX, such as web search, URL opening, code execution, or image generation. They are usually the most direct path.
- Use MCP when there is a set of tools with their own schema, when another system already speaks MCP, or when you want the same server to be used by different clients.

In production, treat the MCP server as an API exposed to an agent:

- Write clear tool descriptions.
- Keep schemas restrictive.
- Configure authentication in the server headers.
- Do not offer overly generic tools such as `execute`, `request`, or `search` without strong descriptions and controlled parameters.

Ambiguous tools increase wrong calls. Specific tools like `lookup_customer_by_email` or `create_support_ticket` help the model decide better.

A long tool list also has a cost: every tool offered to the model adds its name, description, and schema to each request. To measure that overhead and reduce it, see [how to measure and cut tool-definition tokens](https://aivax.net/blog/reduce-mcp-tool-definition-tokens-too-many-tools/).

### Choosing the function name

Use a name that states the action. Keep it simple and deterministic. Avoid names that are hard to guess or that do not hint at the function's role. Otherwise the assistant may not call the function when it should.

For a function that queries a user in an external database, prefer:

- `search_user`
- `query_user`

Avoid:

- `search` (implicit, possibly ambiguous)
- `search user` (name with improper characters)

After the name is settled, write the description.

### Choosing the function description

Use the description to tell the assistant what the function does and when to call it.

Include:

- Scenarios where the assistant should call it.
- Scenarios where it should not be called.
- A few one-shot call examples, or explicit function rules.

### Defining MCP servers

Define MCP servers on the gateway when the assistant should discover and call that server's tools. Send a JSON array:

```json
[
    {
        "name": "My MCP server",
        "url": "https://example-server.io/mcp",
        "headers": {
            "Authorization": "<AIVAX_API_KEY>"
        }
    }
]
```

Your MCP server must support **Streamable HTTP** to work with AIVAX as a gateway tool source. You can define custom headers in your MCP server configuration to set up authentication or other needs. Discovered tools, server instructions, and remote skills are reused for `cacheDuration` seconds; the default is 600.

Each MCP source accepts the following fields. Use them to name the source, authenticate the connection, and control what the model sees:

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | `string` | Required | Display name of the source, with at least 3 characters. It identifies the source in tool names (see `prefixTools`), server instructions, and remote skill descriptions. |
| `url` | `string` | Required | Absolute HTTP or HTTPS URL of the MCP server's Streamable HTTP endpoint. |
| `description` | `string` | `null` | Optional note describing what the source provides. It is informational only: it is not sent to the model or to the MCP server. |
| `headers` | `object` | `{}` | Map of HTTP header names to string values sent on every connection to the server, both during discovery and on each tool call. Use it for authentication, such as `Authorization`. |
| `cacheDuration` | `integer` | `600` | Time, in seconds, that discovered tools, server instructions, and remote skills are reused before AIVAX lists them again. Accepts values from `0` to `86400`. Tool calls are never cached. |
| `prefixTools` | `boolean` | `true` | When `true`, each tool is exposed to the model as `mcp_<source>_<tool>`, where `<source>` is the `name` in lowercase with spaces replaced by hyphens and other non-alphanumeric characters removed. For example, the `get_weather` tool of `My MCP server` becomes `mcp_my-mcp-server_get_weather`. When `false`, the server's original tool name is used; make sure it does not collide with tools from other sources or functions in the same gateway. The server always receives its original tool name. |
| `allowClientInstructions` | `boolean` | `true` | Adds the usage instructions advertised by the server to the gateway context. See [server instructions and remote skills](#server-instructions-and-remote-skills). |
| `allowRemoteSkills` | `boolean` | `true` | Imports verified remote skills from servers that advertise the skills extension. See [server instructions and remote skills](#server-instructions-and-remote-skills). |

If your server targets MCP `2026-07-28`, see [Stateless MCP: migrating off Mcp-Session-Id](https://aivax.net/blog/mcp-stateless-core-moves-session-state-into-your-application/) for how it interacts with this gateway.

## Server instructions and remote skills

Use these options when a trusted MCP server should add instructions or skills to the gateway. Each MCP source accepts `allowClientInstructions` and `allowRemoteSkills`. Both are enabled by default. Set either option to `false` to exclude that content.

Only connect servers whose content you trust:

- Server instructions are added to the gateway context.
- Remote skills become available through `read_skill` alongside your account skills.

To be imported, a server must advertise the `resources` capability and the `io.modelcontextprotocol/skills` extension when the connection is initialized. Remote skills never replace your account skills or same-named skills from another source.

For how skill discovery, verification and activation are split between server and host, and which clients support it, see [MCP skills vs tools](https://aivax.net/blog/mcp-skills-extension-workflows/).

Only each skill's root `SKILL.md` is imported, and it must match the content the server advertised. Supporting files and scripts are not imported, and skill frontmatter does not grant tool permissions: your existing tool policies still apply. Disable remote skills if you need per-skill approval.

Before connecting a third-party server, review [MCP server security best practices for third-party servers](https://aivax.net/blog/mcp-is-a-trust-boundary-not-just-a-tool-catalog/), which covers tool poisoning, credentials, worker-based blocking and server-side approval.

The same options apply to MCP sources added by gateway workers.

## Metadata sent with MCP requests

Use this section when your MCP server must identify the calling context or receive application values with a request.

AIVAX adds the calling context in `params._meta` to every request and notification it sends to the server: `initialize`, `notifications/initialized`, `tools/list`, `skills/list`, `resources/read`, and `tools/call`.

- In `tools/call`, arguments contain the tool input.
- Metadata identifies the calling context and carries application-supplied values.

The following example illustrates a call with an identified user, a conversation token, and custom metadata:

```json
{
    "jsonrpc": "2.0",
    "id": 2,
    "method": "tools/call",
    "params": {
        "name": "get_weather",
        "arguments": {
            "location": "New York"
        },
        "_meta": {
            "_aiv_nonce": "<BCRYPT_HASH>",
            "_aiv_external_user_id": "<EXTERNAL_USER_ID>",
            "_aiv_call_source": "WebChatClient",
            "_aiv_conversation_token": "<CONVERSATION_TOKEN>",
            "_aiv_moment": "2025-09-09T16:58:05.0000000+00:00",
            "tenant_id": "<TENANT_ID>",
            "request_id": "<APPLICATION_REQUEST_ID>"
        }
    }
}
```

### AIVAX fields

These fields identify the calling context. All paths below are relative to `params._meta`. Names beginning with `_aiv` are reserved; do not use them for custom metadata.

| Field | JSON type | Meaning and availability |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `_aiv_nonce` | `string` or `null` | BCrypt hash derived from the calling account's hook key. Without a configured hook key, its value is `null`. Verify the configured plain-text hook key against this hash as described in [hook authentication](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/authentication.md#hook-authentication); do not compare hash strings or expect the hook key itself. |
| `_aiv_external_user_id` | `string` or `null` | External user identifier carried by the inference context. For chat clients it comes from the session; for chat completions it comes from the request's `user` field. It can be `null` when no user was identified. Use it to look up the user in your application, not as an AIVAX account ID or proof of authorization. |
| `_aiv_call_source` | `string` | Origin of the inference, not the outbound tool transport. An MCP tool called during web chat inference still receives `WebChatClient`, not `McpClient`. See the values below. |
| `_aiv_conversation_token` | `string` or `null` | Conversation correlation token. For chat completions, it is the request's `conversation_token`, or the token AIVAX generated when none was sent. It can be `null`. It is not a credential or a unique tool-call ID; calls in the same conversation can share it. |
| `_aiv_moment` | `string` | ISO 8601 timestamp, with a UTC offset, of when AIVAX sent the request. It is not the user's local time. |

### Call source values

Use the source to route and diagnose the call, not to authorize it. The same string values are used by protocol functions in `context.callSource`:

| Value | Inference origin |
| --- | --- |
| `WebChatClient` | AIVAX web chat client. |
| `ChatCompletionsApi` | OpenAI-compatible chat completions API; the default origin for that API. |
| `FunctionsApi` | Functions API. |
| `IntegrationBot` | Messaging integration bot. |
| `OpenWebUiClient` | Open WebUI client. |
| `McpClient` | Inference initiated through an MCP client. |
| `ValidationApi` | Agentic test validation. |

Consumers should tolerate future source values.

### Custom metadata and security

Custom inference metadata is a map of string keys to string values. It comes from request `metadata` for chat completions or session metadata for chat clients, including sessions created by messaging integrations.

AIVAX copies these entries directly into `params._meta`. Custom keys beginning with `_aiv` are ignored. In the example, `tenant_id` and `request_id` are application-defined. There is no nested `metadata` object in the MCP envelope.

Before you rely on metadata:

- Do not send secrets in custom metadata. These values are forwarded to the remote tool server.
- Validate tenant and user access against your own trusted records before using metadata to select data or perform writes.
- Do not treat an external user ID, a conversation token, or a call-source label as permission by itself.
- Treat the nonce as proof of the configured account hook key only. It is not a signature of the arguments, a unique request ID, or a replay-prevention mechanism.
- Keep HTTPS and the MCP server's configured authentication headers.
- Apply your own authorization and duplicate-operation controls.
- If your server requires nonce authentication, reject a missing or invalid nonce.

For the equivalent HTTP callback envelope, see [protocol function context](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/tools/protocol-functions.md#context-fields).

## Tool results

A tool result is what the MCP server returns after a call. AIVAX adds supported blocks back into the conversation so the model can continue.

- Text is added directly to the tool result.
- Image and audio blocks are attached back into the conversation as multimodal content with generated IDs.
- Unsupported content block types are reported as unsupported text.

If something goes wrong, check the symptom:

- **The tool does not appear for the model:** verify that the remote server is reachable, supports Streamable HTTP, has the correct authentication headers, and is configured as an MCP source in the gateway.
- **The tool appears but is not called:** review the name, description, and schema.
- **The tool is called with bad arguments:** restrict the JSON Schema and include property descriptions.
- **The call fails:** make the MCP server return readable errors so the model can decide whether to try another argument, ask the user for information, or stop the action.

---

Source: https://docs.aivax.net/docs/tools/protocol-functions.html

# Protocol Functions

Protocol functions are AIVAX server-side tools. The model requests a named action, and AIVAX executes it from the server by calling your HTTP callback or an internal AIVAX callback URL.

Use them when an assistant needs a controlled way to interact with your application, such as checking an order, opening a support ticket, or querying a private service. The model sees the tool name, description, and JSON argument schema. It does not see the callback URL or headers.

<img src="/assets/diagrams/protocol-functions-1.drawio.svg">

A protocol function has two contracts:

- **The model contract:** the public tool name, description, and JSON Schema that guide the model's tool call.
- **The callback contract:** the hidden URL and optional headers that AIVAX uses to execute the tool after the model calls it.

This separation keeps implementation details out of the prompt while still giving the model a precise capability to use.

## When to use protocol functions

Use protocol functions to expose a specific HTTP action to an AI Gateway without building a full MCP server. They fit point integrations, such as fetching a user, registering a lead, or invoking an internal automation. AIVAX keeps the URL hidden from the model, sends the request from the server side, and adds the textual result to the conversation context.

Protocol functions sit between other tool types: they are simpler than [MCP](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/tools/mcp.md) and more specific than [workers](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/workers.md), while still giving the model a controlled tool for an external action. Use this rule of thumb:

| Need | Prefer |
|---|---|
| One or a few stable HTTP callbacks owned by your app | Protocol functions |
| A larger tool catalog, standardized discovery, or an existing MCP server | [MCP](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/tools/mcp.md) |
| Web search, URL reading, code execution, image generation, memory, or HTTP request tools maintained by AIVAX | [Built-in tools](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/tools/builtin-tools.md) |
| Event-time policy, message rewriting, dynamic tool injection, or blocking a tool call before execution | [Workers](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/workers.md) |
| Provider-native tool definitions that your own client will execute | Raw `tools` in an OpenAI-compatible request |

Every protocol function has four parts:

- **Name**: helps the model recognize the action. It must be a valid JavaScript identifier with at least three characters.
- **Description**: tells the model when to call the function.
- **Argument schema** (`contentFormat`): limits the format of the arguments.
- **Callback URL** (`callbackUrl`): where AIVAX sends the call. The model never sees it or its authentication details.

Because the callback stays hidden, you can create specialized tools without exposing internal endpoints. Your service must still validate the `X-Request-Nonce`, validate the received arguments, and apply its own authorization when the call depends on the user.

### Choosing the function name

The function name should be simple and specific about what the function does. Avoid names that are hard to guess or that do not reflect the function's role, because the assistant may not call the function when it should.

For example, consider a function that queries a user in an external database. Good names include:

- `search_user`
- `query_user`

Weak names include:

- `search` (too broad)
- `query_user_in_database_data` (long and noisy)
- `pesquisa-usuario` (name not in English)
- `search user` (name with improper characters)

### Choosing the function description

The function description should explain what the function does, when the assistant should call it, and when it should not call it. Good descriptions include the expected input, the kind of result returned, and any decision rule the assistant should follow before calling the tool.

For example, a useful description is:

> Use this tool to fetch a customer profile by customer ID when the user asks about account status, recent orders, or support eligibility. Do not call it when the user only provides a name or email; ask for the customer ID first.

That gives the model a clear action, trigger, and limitation. A vague description such as "Search customers" gives the model much less guidance.

## Defining protocol functions

Protocol functions are defined in the [AI Gateway](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/ai-gateways/concepts.md). You can declare them directly in the gateway when the list is stable, or provide a remote source that returns the function list when the catalog is managed by another service.

The direct form is the simplest option. Use it when the function list changes rarely and belongs to the gateway configuration itself.

Reference:

[API endpoint reference](https://inference.aivax.net/apidocs?embed=iframe&embed-endpoint=Create%20AI%20Gateway)

```json
{
    "name": "my-ai-gateway",
    "parameters": {
        "baseAddress": "@integrated",
        "modelName": "@openai/gpt-5-mini",
        "protocolFunctions": [
            {
                "name": "list_clients",
                "description": "Use this tool to list and search for the user's clients.",
                "callbackUrl": "https://my-external-api.com/api/scp/users",
                "contentFormat": {
                    "type": "object",
                    "properties": {}
                }
            },
            {
                "name": "view_client",
                "description": "Use this tool to obtain details and orders of a client via its ID.",
                "callbackUrl": "https://my-external-api.com/api/scp/users",
                "contentFormat": {
                    "type": "object",
                    "properties": {
                        "user_id": {
                            "type": "string",
                            "format": "uuid"
                        }
                    },
                    "required": ["user_id"]
                }
            }
        ]
    }
}
```

In the snippet above, the gateway exposes `list_clients` and `view_client` to the model. The model decides whether to call one of them during generation. If it calls `view_client`, AIVAX validates the arguments against `contentFormat`, then sends the callback request to your service, as described in [Handling function calls](#handling-function-calls).

> [!IMPORTANT]
>
> Every function definition, including its name, description, and schema, consumes input tokens. The more functions you define, the more input tokens you consume.

## Protocol function sources

Protocol function sources let a gateway load its protocol functions from one or more remote endpoints instead of storing every function inline. Use sources when the function catalog belongs to another service, changes independently from the gateway, or is shared by multiple gateways.

- Use inline `protocolFunctions` for stable, gateway-owned tools.
- Use `protocolFunctionSources` for remotely managed catalogs. It is an array of URL strings, not an array of source objects.

You can use both in the same gateway. Function names must remain unique after inline functions, sourced functions, MCP tools, built-in tools, and raw tools are combined.

Each source URL is an HTTP endpoint that returns a JSON object with a `functions` array. AIVAX fetches the source before each inference and converts each returned definition into a server-side tool. Definitions are reused for up to 10 minutes, so catalog changes can take that long to appear.

<img src="/assets/diagrams/protocol-functions-2.drawio.svg">

Define the function listing endpoints in your AI Gateway:

```json
{
    "name": "my-ai-gateway",
    "parameters": {
        "baseAddress": "@integrated",
        "modelName": "@openai/gpt-5-mini",
        "protocolFunctionSources": [
            "https://my-external-api.com/api/scp/listings"
        ]
    }
}
```

The function source endpoint receives a `GET` request. It must return a successful HTTP status and a JSON object in this format:

<div class="request-item get">
    <span>GET</span>
    <span>
        https://my-external-api.com/api/scp/listings
    </span>
</div>

```json
{
    "functions": [
        {
            "name": "list_clients",
            "description": "Use this tool to list and search for the user's clients.",
            "callbackUrl": "https://my-external-api.com/api/scp/users",
            "contentFormat": {
                "type": "object",
                "properties": {}
            }
        },
        {
            "name": "view_client",
            "description": "Use this tool to obtain details and orders of a client via its ID.",
            "callbackUrl": "https://my-external-api.com/api/scp/users",
            "contentFormat": {
                "type": "object",
                "properties": {
                    "user_id": {
                        "type": "string",
                        "format": "uuid"
                    }
                },
                "required": ["user_id"]
            }
        }
    ]
}
```

The returned function objects use the same shape as inline `protocolFunctions`: `name`, `description`, `callbackUrl`, optional `headers`, and `contentFormat`.

If the source endpoint returns a non-success status, the inference request fails. Make the source endpoint fast, stable, and small enough to return only the functions the gateway should expose. If the catalog is user- or tenant-specific, use the request nonce and your own authorization rules to decide which functions to return.

## Handling function calls

When the model calls a function, inline or sourced, AIVAX sends an HTTP `POST` request to its `callbackUrl` with `Content-Type: application/json` and a body equivalent to:

```json
{
    "type": "tool_call",
    "function": {
        "name": "view_client",
        "content": {
            "user_id": "example-user-id"
        }
    },
    "context": {
        "externalUserId": "<EXTERNAL_USER_ID>",
        "metadata": {
            "tenant_id": "<TENANT_ID>",
            "request_id": "<APPLICATION_REQUEST_ID>"
        },
        "callSource": "WebChatClient",
        "conversationToken": "<CONVERSATION_TOKEN>",
        "moment": "2025-05-18T03:36:27+00:00"
    }
}
```

`function.content` holds the model-generated arguments, and `context` describes the inference that triggered the call.

Your callback must return a successful HTTP status (2xx), even when the assistant made a mistake in the call. On a non-success response, the model receives a generic tool-call error instead of your response body.

### Context fields

`context` is built by AIVAX, separately from the model-generated arguments in `function.content`. Use it to correlate the request with your application.

| Field | JSON type | Meaning and availability |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `context.externalUserId` | `string` or `null` | External user identifier from the inference context. For a [chat session](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/chat-clients/managing-sessions.md#identify-users-with-a-tag), this is the session's external user ID; for chat completions, it comes from the request's `user` field. It can be `null` when no user was identified. It is not an AIVAX account ID or an authentication credential. |
| `context.metadata` | `object` | Application-supplied string key/value pairs from the inference request or chat session. For chat completions, these are the request's `metadata` entries. The object is empty (`{}`) when none are supplied. The example's `tenant_id` and `request_id` are custom fields, not names generated by AIVAX. |
| `context.callSource` | `string` | Origin of the inference, such as `WebChatClient`, `ChatCompletionsApi`, or `IntegrationBot`. It does not describe the callback transport. See the shared [call source values](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/tools/mcp.md#call-source-values) for all current values. |
| `context.conversationToken` | `string` or `null` | Conversation correlation token. For chat completions, it is the request's `conversation_token`, or the token AIVAX generated when none was sent. It can be `null`. It is not a credential or a unique callback ID; calls in the same conversation can share it. |
| `context.moment` | `string` | JSON date-time timestamp, with a UTC offset, of when AIVAX prepared the callback. It is not the user's local time. |

Custom metadata stays nested under `context.metadata`; it is not merged into `context`. This differs from [MCP metadata](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/tools/mcp.md#metadata-sent-with-mcp-requests), where the same custom entries sit alongside reserved `_aiv_*` fields in `params._meta`.

The authentication nonce is **not** a `context` or `metadata` field. Protocol functions receive it in the `X-Request-Nonce` HTTP header when the account has a hook key. MCP tool calls carry the equivalent value in `params._meta._aiv_nonce` instead. These context fields describe execution POST requests; do not assume that function source-listing requests have this JSON body.

### Response format

Return a textual response body. AIVAX attaches it to the conversation as the function result exactly as your endpoint returns it. No JSON structure is required, but a short, human-readable answer is easiest for the assistant to use.

Write the response for the model, not for the end user. It may contain data, warnings, and short instructions on how to use the result. For example:

- If an order search finds the order, return its status, expected date, and relevant restrictions.
- If the order is not found, say so and indicate which data the assistant should ask the user for.

Expected errors, such as a client ID that does not exist or a field in the wrong format, are common. Return them with a 2xx status and describe the error and how the assistant can work around it in the response body.

Avoid returning huge objects, HTML, raw logs, or internal messages. This content enters the context and can confuse the next response.

AIVAX validates arguments against the JSON Schema before execution. Your callback should still validate them, because a schema limits structure but cannot replace business authorization or consistency checks. Functions that take no arguments should use an empty object schema.

### Authentication

Request authentication is done via the `X-Request-Nonce` header sent in protocol function calls and source-listing requests.

See the [authentication](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/authentication.md) manual to understand how to authenticate reverse requests from AIVAX.

### User authentication

Use `context.externalUserId` to look up the caller in your application, then check whether that user may access the requested resource or perform the requested action. If a function requires an identified user, reject calls without a usable identifier rather than silently granting anonymous access.

Validate the nonce and enforce your own user and tenant authorization rules. Request and session metadata can contain caller-supplied values: a `tenant_id`, `callSource`, or `conversationToken` is not proof of permission. Avoid putting secrets in metadata because it is forwarded to your callback. The nonce verifies the account hook key, not the individual user's permissions, and does not sign the body or prevent replay; use your own duplicate-operation controls for writes. For a worked pattern that derives an operation key and returns the stored result on repeats, see [how to make LLM tool calls idempotent](https://aivax.net/blog/make-llm-tool-calls-idempotent-protocol-functions/).

### Security considerations

The model sees only the function's name, description, and argument schema. It cannot see the callback endpoint or the callback headers configured for the function. Treat all callback requests as privileged server-to-server calls: validate the nonce, validate arguments, enforce authorization, and avoid exposing broad write actions unless your application has its own approval rules.

## Specialist functions

Specialist functions are protocol functions whose callback is an AIVAX capability instead of your own endpoint. Unlike [built-in tools](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/tools/builtin-tools.md), you name and describe them yourself, so you can point several functions at different resources in your AIVAX account.

Define a specialist function by setting `callbackUrl` to an `aivax://` URL:

```json
{
    "name": "my-ai-gateway",
    "parameters": {
        "baseAddress": "@integrated",
        "modelName": "@openai/gpt-5-mini",
        "protocolFunctions": [
            {
                "name": "search_disease",
                "description": "Use this tool to search for diseases, treatments, and symptoms.",
                "callbackUrl": "aivax://query-collection?collection-id=your-collection-id&top=5&min=0.4",
                "contentFormat": {
                    "type": "object",
                    "properties": {
                        "query": {
                            "type": "string",
                            "description": "Name of the disease, treatment, or symptoms."
                        }
                    },
                    "required": [
                        "query"
                    ]
                }
            }
        ]
    }
}
```

This function lets the model query a specific [document collection](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/rag/collections.md). Its description tells the assistant what to search in that collection and what to expect back. Define one function per collection to give an assistant several sources of specialist content.

The JSON Schema structure of a specialist function is fixed, but you can customize its property descriptions. Specialist function settings are passed as query parameters in the URL.

Currently, only one specialist function exists:

- `query-collection`: performs a RAG search on a specified collection.

Query parameters:

- `collection-id`: the UUID of the collection to be searched.
- `top`: a number indicating how many documents should be returned in the search.
- `min`: a decimal indicating the minimum similarity score of the search.
- `refs`: when present, includes referenced parent documents in the RAG result.

Function JSON format:

```json
{
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
        "query": {
            "type": "string",
            "description": "Search content."
        }
    },
    "required": [
        "query"
    ]
}
```

---

Source: https://docs.aivax.net/docs/tools/shell.html

# Shell Sandboxing

AIVAX offers a virtual shell environment that can be used by agent assistants to execute terminal commands during inference. This feature is especially useful for tasks such as data manipulation, API calls, script execution, and workflows that are easier to express as command-line operations.

The shell environment allows moving selected model tools to the shell side, turning them into CLI commands. This is useful when you have many tools and do not want to expose all of them directly to the model, or when a tool is easier to use through command-line arguments and pipes.

When enabled in an AI Gateway, the model sees a `shell` tool with one argument: `command`. Commands run in a sandboxed shell with a workspace mounted at `/home/workspace`. Each command has a time limit and a cap on the output returned to the model; see [Pricing and limits](#pricing-and-limits).

## Design for the limits

The command timeout and output cap shape how shell tools should behave. Keep commands fast and their output narrow: filter server-side with `grep`, `awk`, or query flags before printing, and prefer tools that return CSV or line-delimited rows the model can slice with pipes. When a result legitimately exceeds the cap, split the work — one command to list or count, follow-ups to fetch slices — or write the full output to a workspace file and read the relevant part back through the Shell file API below.

Long-running operations do not belong in an inference command. Move exports, bulk transforms, and polling loops to [Batch](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/batch.md) or an external job, and let the shell handle the interactive slices.

## Adapting tools for shell

In the virtual shell interface, standard command-line utilities and registered shell modules are available. This way, you can adapt your tools to return raw or long outputs, and the model can use the shell's text manipulation tools to extract the relevant information, for example:

```bash
get-users --filter active --format csv | grep "John Doe" | awk -F, '{print $1, $2}'
```

In the line above, `get-users` is a custom tool that returns a list of users in CSV format. The `grep` command filters the results to find "John Doe", and `awk` extracts and formats the desired columns. This tool may have been defined by [MCP](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/tools/mcp.md), [built-in tools](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/tools/builtin-tools.md) or be a [protocol tool](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/tools/protocol-functions.md).

Tools moved into the shell are no longer exposed as direct model functions, except reserved tools such as `shell` and `read_skill`. Configure the shell tool list as either:

- `WhiteList`: only listed tools are exposed as shell commands.
- `BlackList`: listed tools remain direct model tools, and the other non-reserved tools are exposed as shell commands.

Use the runtime function name when listing tools, such as `web_search`, `open_url`, `request`, or a protocol/MCP function name. Each shell command generated from a tool supports `--help` and maps JSON Schema properties to command-line options.

Prefer the whitelist when the model needs a small, predictable command set. Prefer the blacklist when most tools are shell-friendly and only a few must stay as direct functions.

## Data persistence

It is possible to define data persistence for the shell environment. When `allowDataPersistence` is enabled and the inference context has a user external ID, AIVAX mounts a persistent workspace scoped to the account and user. This allows the agent to keep files across conversations and sessions for that identified user.

If persistence is disabled, or the inference context has no user external ID, the shell uses an in-memory filesystem and the workspace is discarded after the inference iteration.

Enable persistence only for data the user expects to survive — working documents, generated reports, configuration they manage. Keep secrets, credentials, and other users' data out of the persistent workspace: anything written there endures beyond the session that created it.

## Internet access

By default, the shell has internet access through `curl`, `wget` and `ping`. Set `bashOptions.allowInternetAccess` to `false` to remove the network commands and run fully offline.

## Pricing and limits

The number of Bash commands per hour depends on the plan; see [Built-in tools and web search limits](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/limits.md#built-in-tools-and-web-search). These limits apply to every plan:

| Limit | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Time per command | 60 seconds |
| Output returned to the model | 4,096 characters |
| Shell file API upload | 100 MB maximum request body |

## Shell file API

AIVAX also exposes Shell I/O endpoints under `/api/v1/shell/io` for authenticated accounts. Every request requires the `X-Shell-User-Id` header, which scopes the filesystem sandbox the endpoint operates on.

With these endpoints, you can list directories, download files, inspect file metadata, create temporary public file addresses, upload files, create directories, and delete files or directories. Uploads have a maximum request body size; see [Pricing and limits](#pricing-and-limits).

Reference:

[API endpoint reference](https://inference.aivax.net/apidocs?embed=iframe&embed-endpoint=List%20Directory)
[API endpoint reference](https://inference.aivax.net/apidocs?embed=iframe&embed-endpoint=Download%20File)
[API endpoint reference](https://inference.aivax.net/apidocs?embed=iframe&embed-endpoint=Get%20File%20Details)
[API endpoint reference](https://inference.aivax.net/apidocs?embed=iframe&embed-endpoint=Get%20File%20Public%20Address)
[API endpoint reference](https://inference.aivax.net/apidocs?embed=iframe&embed-endpoint=Upload%20File)
[API endpoint reference](https://inference.aivax.net/apidocs?embed=iframe&embed-endpoint=Create%20Directory)
[API endpoint reference](https://inference.aivax.net/apidocs?embed=iframe&embed-endpoint=Delete%20File)
[API endpoint reference](https://inference.aivax.net/apidocs?embed=iframe&embed-endpoint=Delete%20Directory)

---

Source: https://docs.aivax.net/docs/mcp-utilities/collections-mcp.html

# Collections and RAG MCP

The Collections MCP exposes one or more AIVAX RAG collections as tools for compatible MCP clients. Use it when an external model, agent, IDE, or desktop assistant should decide when to search an AIVAX knowledge base.

For a typical AIVAX chat client, it is often simpler to attach the collection directly to an [AI Gateway](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/inference/ai-gateways/concepts.md) and let the gateway RAG pipeline retrieve documents automatically.

For information about creating collections, preparing documents, and improving retrieval quality, see [Collections](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/rag/collections.md), [Documents](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/rag/documents.md), and [Semantic Search](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/rag/semantic-search.md).

## Endpoint

```text
https://inference.aivax.net/v1/mcp/collections
```

## Headers

| Header | Description | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Authorization` | Bearer token of your API key. | Required |
| `X-Mcp-Collection-Id` | One or more collection IDs. Use commas for multiple collections. | Required |
| `X-Mcp-Collection-Name` | Collection name used to generate tool names. | `collection` |
| `X-Mcp-Reranker` | Selects the ranker used to order search results. Use a canonical `@provider/name`, `lexical`, `rrf`, `smart`, or `none`. | `@aivax/reflex-v1` |
| `X-Mcp-Top-K` | Maximum number of results to return. | `5` |
| `X-Mcp-Min-Score` | Minimum relevance score greater than 0 and up to 1.0. | `0.4` |
| `X-Mcp-Use-References` | Set to `none` to enable references in search results; omit the header to disable them. | disabled |
| `X-Mcp-Allow-Write` | Use `yes` to expose document write and delete tools. | disabled |
| `X-Mcp-Naming-Convention` | Controls how generated tools are named. Use `default` or `agent`. | `default` |
| `X-Mcp-Enabled-Tools` | Comma-separated allowlist of tool types to expose: `search`, `browse`, `get`, `write`, `delete`. See [Select which tools are exposed](#select-which-tools-are-exposed). | all available tools |

## Configuration example

Visual Studio Code:

```json
{
  "servers": {
    "my-rag-collection-mcp": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "https://inference.aivax.net/v1/mcp/collections",
      "headers": {
        "Authorization": "Bearer <AIVAX_API_KEY>",
        "X-Mcp-Collection-Id": "<COLLECTION_ID>",
        "X-Mcp-Collection-Name": "my_collection",
        "X-Mcp-Top-K": "5",
        "X-Mcp-Min-Score": "0.4",
        // Enables references in search results.
        "X-Mcp-Use-References": "none"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

## Generated tools

The server generates up to five tools per configuration: search, browse, get document, and, when writes are allowed, write and delete. Tool names are built from `X-Mcp-Collection-Name` and the naming convention.

### Search tool

With the default naming convention, the read tool is named:

```text
{collection_name}_search
```

It accepts:

- `search_terms` (`string[]`): one or more search terms.
- `filter` (`string`, optional): a [document filter](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/rag/document-filters.md) applied before the semantic search, such as `tags has "faq" and updatedAt >= now-30d`.

The MCP read tool accepts at most 10 search terms and 500 total characters per call.

### Browse tool

The browse tool lists indexed documents in a fixed order, without semantic search. Use it when the model needs to see what a collection contains, page through every document, or read a document by its exact name. With the default naming convention, it is named:

```text
{collection_name}_browse_documents
```

With the `agent` naming convention, it is named `{collection_name}_list`. It accepts:

- `filter` (`string`, optional): a [document filter](https://docs.aivax.net/docs/rag/document-filters.md), such as `name = "setup.md"`, `reference = "manual-v2"`, or `tags has "faq"`.
- `sort` (`string`, optional): `createdAt`, `updatedAt`, `indexedAt`, or `name`. Defaults to `createdAt`.
- `descending` (`boolean`, optional): lists newest first, or from Z to A when sorting by name. Defaults to `false`.
- `include_content` (`boolean`, optional): adds the content and metadata of each document. Defaults to `false`, so the tool returns only names, tags, references, and dates. To read one document, prefer the get document tool.
- `limit` (`number`, optional): documents per page, from 1 to 50. Defaults to 20.
